7.about: Op. 7 was the longest sonata Beethoven had yet written, and only the Hammerklavier would surpass it. The first movement, in a vigorous 6/8, is driven by pulsing repeated notes and brilliant, orchestral passagework that seems always to press forward. The Largo, con gran espressione, in C major, is the heart of the work: its phrases are broken by long silences, so that the music seems to speak, pause and reflect. The third movement is a minuet-like Allegro whose E-flat-minor trio is a shadowy stream of triplets, and the finale is an affectionate rondo, briefly threatened by a violent C-minor episode. The whole sonata claims for the piano the ambition of a symphony.
7.ctx: Published by Artaria in 1797, Op. 7 was issued on its own rather than in a set — a sign that Beethoven considered it a major statement. Its dedicatee, Countess Babette von Keglevics, was his piano pupil; after her marriage to Prince Innocenzo Odescalchi he also dedicated the First Piano Concerto to her. The first edition called it a ‘Grande Sonate’, and a later nickname, ‘Die Verliebte’ (The Maiden in Love), may reflect rumours of Beethoven’s affection for his pupil. It dates from the time of his 1796 tour to Prague, Dresden, Leipzig and Berlin, when he was becoming known as a composer as well as a pianist.
parts: An expansive, energetic opening movement in 6/8 metre.
A solemn movement in which silence is as eloquent as sound.
A minuet-like movement with a turbulent, shadowy trio.
A warm, flowing rondo with a stormy C-minor episode.
facts: It was the first of his sonatas to be published on its own rather than in a set.
The dedicatee, Babette von Keglevics, also received the dedication of the First Piano Concerto.
Henle rates it level 8, the highest of the pre-1800 sonatas.

13.about: The ‘Pathétique’ opens with a weighty Grave introduction of dramatic dotted rhythms and sighing phrases, then plunges into a stormy Allegro di molto e con brio over a rumbling tremolo bass. The Grave returns twice within the Allegro — at the start of the development and before the coda — binding introduction and movement into a single drama. The Adagio cantabile in A-flat major is a noble, songful rondo whose theme recalls the slow movement of Mozart’s C-minor Sonata, K. 457, and its warmth gives essential relief between two stormy movements. The finale, a restless C-minor rondo, shares its melodic shape with the first movement’s second theme, tying the sonata together.
13.ctx: Composed in 1797–98 and published in 1799, the sonata was dedicated to Prince Karl von Lichnowsky, Beethoven’s patron and host in his early Vienna years. The title ‘Grande Sonate pathétique’ appeared on the first edition, probably with Beethoven’s approval. Its intensity made it a sensation: Ignaz Moscheles recalled that as a boy he was forbidden by his teacher to play such ‘eccentric’ music, and copied it out in secret. Widely arranged and imitated, it became one of Beethoven’s most popular works in his lifetime, and its C-minor drama left its mark on Romantic sonatas by Schubert, Mendelssohn and Chopin.
parts: Grave – Allegro di molto e con brio
A weighty introduction whose chords return to interrupt the stormy Allegro.
A songful rondo with a warm, singing theme.
An agitated rondo with a flowing, contrapuntal episode.
facts: The slow introduction returns within the fast movement — an unusual structural idea.
Ignaz Moscheles recalled being forbidden to play it as a student because it was considered too eccentric.
Henle lists it at ABRSM Grade 8/ARSM level.

15.about: A bright, festive concerto with trumpets and timpani. The orchestra opens with a march-like theme, but the piano enters with a new melody of its own rather than repeating it, and goes on to dazzle with rapid scales and arpeggios. The Largo in A-flat major is a long, lyrical movement in which the piano sings in intimate dialogue with the clarinet. The rondo finale, Allegro scherzando, is full of high spirits and syncopated wit, bringing the work to a joyful close.
15.ctx: Although numbered first, this concerto was written after the one now known as No. 2; it was simply published first, by Mollo in 1801. Beethoven played it himself in his early Vienna years — possibly first in 1795 — and in Prague in 1798, revising it along the way. Years later he wrote three cadenzas for the first movement, one of them very long. It was dedicated to Princess Barbara Odescalchi, his former pupil Babette von Keglevics, who had also received the Sonata Op. 7. The concerto established Beethoven as Mozart’s successor in the genre.
parts: A grand, military-flavoured opening with brilliant piano writing.
A serene, song-like movement with prominent clarinet.
15.sc: Piano, flute, 2 oboes, 2 clarinets, 2 bassoons, 2 horns, 2 trumpets, timpani, strings
facts: It was composed after the Second Concerto.
Beethoven wrote three different cadenzas for the first movement.
The dedicatee was also the dedicatee of the Sonata Op. 7.

16.about: A quintet for piano, oboe, clarinet, horn and bassoon, modelled on Mozart’s Quintet K. 452 for the same combination, which Mozart had called the best thing he had yet written. It follows its model in three movements: a stately slow introduction leading to a spacious Allegro, a lyrical Andante cantabile in which each wind instrument takes a turn with the melody, and a genial rondo finale with a hunting flavour. The piano leads throughout, reflecting Beethoven’s own role as performer, while the winds supply colour and warmth.
16.ctx: Beethoven wrote the quintet in 1796 and played it in Vienna the following year; he also published a version for piano and string trio. According to Ferdinand Ries, at one performance Beethoven launched into a long improvisation just before the return of the rondo theme, leaving the wind players waiting with their instruments raised — to their annoyance and the audience’s amusement. It was published in 1801 with a dedication to Prince Joseph zu Schwarzenberg.
parts: A slow introduction and a genial Allegro.
facts: It is modelled on Mozart’s K. 452.
Beethoven also arranged it for piano quartet.
Ries recalled Beethoven improvising at length during a performance.

19.about: The earliest of Beethoven’s piano concertos, though published second, is lighter and more Mozartian than those that followed, and uses no clarinets, trumpets or timpani. The first movement’s long, elegant orchestral opening gives way to a more intimate theme when the piano enters. The Adagio in E-flat major is one of the most expressive slow movements of Beethoven’s early years, closing with a hushed, recitative-like passage for the piano marked ‘con gran espressione’. The rondo finale has a cheeky theme full of off-beat accents that gives it a rustic, playful character.
19.ctx: Beethoven began the concerto in Bonn around 1787–89 and kept revising it as a vehicle for his career as a pianist in Vienna, where he probably played it at his public debut in March 1795. Its original finale was replaced; the discarded movement survives as the Rondo in B-flat, WoO 6. Beethoven told his publisher it was not one of his best works and sold it cheaply to Hoffmeister, who published it in 1801. In 1809 he wrote a new cadenza for the first movement in his mature style.
parts: A slow, deeply expressive movement ending with a recitative.
A playful rondo with a hopping, syncopated theme.
19.sc: Piano, flute, 2 oboes, 2 bassoons, 2 horns, strings
facts: It is his earliest surviving piano concerto.
It uses no clarinets, trumpets or timpani.
Beethoven described it as not one of his best works.

20.about: A sunny, six-movement divertimento for clarinet, horn, bassoon, violin, viola, cello and double bass, in the tradition of the serenades played at Viennese social gatherings. A slow introduction leads to a bright Allegro, followed by a songful Adagio cantabile led by the clarinet, a minuet whose theme Beethoven borrowed from his own Piano Sonata Op. 49 No. 2, a set of variations, a lively scherzo, and a finale with a virtuosic cadenza for the violin. Its melodic charm made it one of the most popular works of Beethoven’s lifetime.
20.ctx: Beethoven introduced the Septet at his first benefit concert on 2 April 1800 at the Burgtheater, alongside the First Symphony, and dedicated it to Empress Maria Theresa, wife of Emperor Francis II. It was an immediate hit and was widely arranged for other combinations — so popular that it came to irritate Beethoven, who reportedly wished it could be destroyed. Its scoring and scale inspired Schubert’s Octet of 1824, written for a patron who wanted a work like Beethoven’s.
parts: A slow introduction and a lively Allegro.
A minuet using the theme of the Sonata Op. 49 No. 2.
Andante con moto alla marcia – Presto
A march and a brilliant finale.
20.sc: Clarinet, horn, bassoon, violin, viola, cello, double bass
facts: It inspired Schubert’s Octet.
Beethoven later resented its popularity.
It was dedicated to Empress Maria Theresa.

21.about: Beethoven’s First Symphony looks back to Haydn and Mozart while announcing a new voice. Its very first chord is a dominant seventh pulling towards F major rather than the home key of C — a harmonic surprise that caused comment in its day. The Allegro con brio is compact and energetic, with prominent wind writing that some critics found noisy. The Andante cantabile con moto begins with a gentle fugal entry in the second violins, and the third movement, though labelled Menuetto, is really a fast scherzo. The finale opens with a famous joke — the violins creep up the scale a few notes at a time, as if unsure of themselves — before bursting into a sparkling Allegro.
21.ctx: Beethoven was 29 when he completed his First Symphony, late compared with Mozart and Haydn — a sign of how seriously he approached the genre. It was premiered on 2 April 1800 at the Burgtheater, at the first public concert he organised for his own benefit, alongside the Septet, a Mozart symphony, excerpts from Haydn’s Creation and a piano concerto played by Beethoven himself. The Leipzig Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung praised its art, novelty and wealth of ideas, while complaining of too much wind. It was dedicated to Baron Gottfried van Swieten, who had introduced Mozart and Haydn to the music of Bach and Handel.
parts: A slow introduction that starts off-key, then a brisk, confident Allegro.
A graceful movement with gentle fugal entries and soft timpani.
A minuet in name only — really Beethoven’s first symphonic scherzo.
A tongue-in-cheek introduction leads to a sparkling, Haydnesque finale.
21.sc: 2 flutes, 2 oboes, 2 clarinets, 2 bassoons, 2 horns, 2 trumpets, timpani, strings
facts: Its opening chord is in the ‘wrong’ key, a famous harmonic joke.
The premiere concert also included the Septet and a Mozart symphony.
Beethoven was nearly 30 when it was premiered.

22.about: A confident, four-movement sonata in B-flat major and the summit of Beethoven’s early classical style. The first movement is energetic and brilliant, its vigorous theme developed with great resourcefulness. The Adagio con molta espressione in E-flat major is a broad, singing movement in the manner of an operatic aria, full of rich harmony and demanding careful control of tone. The Menuetto is graceful, with a stormy G-minor trio of rushing notes, and the finale is a relaxed, songful rondo balanced by a turbulent minor-key episode full of counterpoint. It shows Beethoven entirely at ease with the classical sonata, just before he began to reshape it.
22.ctx: Composed in 1800, the year of the First Symphony and the Septet, the sonata was offered to the Leipzig publisher Franz Anton Hoffmeister in a letter in which Beethoven called it a sonata that ‘hat sich gewaschen’ — Viennese slang for a first-rate piece. He asked 20 ducats for it, the same as for the symphony and the Septet. Published in 1802 with a dedication to Count Johann Georg von Browne, it was the last sonata he wrote in the traditional mould; by then he was already experimenting with form in Op. 26 and Op. 27.
parts: A broad, singing movement in the style of an operatic aria.
A graceful minuet with a stormy G-minor trio.
A relaxed, songful rondo with a contrapuntal minor-key episode.
facts: Beethoven described it as a sonata that ‘hat sich gewaschen’ (has washed itself), meaning first-class.
It marks the end of his early classical period in the sonatas.
Henle rates it level 7.

23.about: A nervous, terse sonata in A minor, in three movements. The first, a Presto in 6/8, is quick and restless, with a driving rhythm and sudden dynamic contrasts. In place of a slow movement comes an Andante scherzoso, più Allegretto — a half-humorous piece in A major with fugal touches. The finale, Allegro molto, is a quick rondo with an undercurrent of melancholy that ends quietly rather than in triumph, confirming the sonata’s uneasy mood.
23.ctx: Beethoven intended this sonata and the ‘Spring’ to appear together as Op. 23, but the violin parts of the two works were engraved in different formats, so they were published separately in 1801 and the ‘Spring’ became Op. 24. Both were dedicated to Count Moritz von Fries, a wealthy banker and patron who later received the dedication of the Seventh Symphony. Written as a pair, the two sonatas make a striking contrast: this one dark and restless, its companion warm and sunny.
facts: It was meant to be published together with the ‘Spring’ Sonata.
It has no true slow movement.
The dedicatee, Count Moritz von Fries, also received the Seventh Symphony.

24.about: One of Beethoven’s sunniest works, and his first violin sonata in four movements. It opens with the violin singing a long, flowing melody over rippling piano accompaniment. The Adagio molto espressivo is calm and songful, its melodies gently decorated on each return. The tiny scherzo contains a famous joke in which the violin seems to lag a beat behind the piano, and the rondo finale is relaxed and happy, with a warm, lyrical theme. Its lyricism and charm have made it one of the most popular violin sonatas ever written.
24.ctx: Composed in 1800–01, the ‘Spring’ was meant to be published with its A-minor companion as a single opus, until an engraving problem separated them. Both were dedicated to Count Moritz von Fries. The nickname was added after Beethoven’s death, probably because of the work’s fresh, lyrical character. Written as Beethoven was establishing himself as the leading composer in Vienna, it remains, with the ‘Kreutzer’, the most frequently performed of his ten violin sonatas.
parts: A flowing, lyrical movement that opens with a violin song.
A tiny scherzo where the violin seems to lag behind.
facts: The scherzo’s rhythmic joke has the violin sounding a beat behind the piano.
The nickname ‘Spring’ is not Beethoven’s.
It is his first violin sonata in four movements.

26.about: An unconventional sonata that abandons the usual fast–slow–fast plan. It opens with five variations on a gentle, lyrical theme, including a dark minor-key variation. A brisk scherzo follows, then a funeral march ‘on the death of a hero’ in A-flat minor, whose drum-roll tremolos and trumpet-like fanfares imitate orchestral sounds on the piano. The finale, a light perpetual motion of running semiquavers, provides a surprising contrast after the march’s gravity. The unusual order gives the sonata the character of a sequence of scenes rather than a classical argument.
26.ctx: Composed in 1800–01 and published in 1802, the sonata was dedicated to Prince Karl von Lichnowsky. Its funeral march may have been prompted by one in Ferdinando Paër’s opera Achille, which Beethoven admired, and it foreshadows the funeral march of the Eroica. Beethoven orchestrated it in 1815 for incidental music to Friedrich Duncker’s play Leonore Prohaska, and it was played in an arrangement at his own funeral in 1827. Chopin admired and taught this sonata, and its march is often seen as an ancestor of the one in his Sonata in B-flat minor.
parts: Five variations on a warm, lyrical theme.
A brisk scherzo with a smooth trio.
Marcia funebre sulla morte d’un eroe
A solemn funeral march with imitated drum rolls and trumpet calls.
A perpetual-motion finale of running semiquavers.
facts: The funeral march was orchestrated by Beethoven in 1815 and played at his own funeral.
It has no conventional fast first movement.
Henle lists it at ABRSM ARSM level.

28.about: A calm, rural-sounding sonata in D major, built over long pedal notes like a drone. The first movement opens with a repeated D in the bass, over which a gentle melody unfolds; the development builds to a climax before subsiding. The Andante in D minor has a walking bass and a folk-like melody, and Czerny recalled that Beethoven loved to play it. The Scherzo draws its humour from repeated single notes, and the finale is a rocking, bagpipe-like rondo that ends with a brilliant coda, Più allegro quasi presto.
28.ctx: Composed in 1801, the same year as the ‘Moonlight’ Sonata, this work shows the other side of Beethoven at the time: serene and unhurried. It was published in 1802 with a dedication to Joseph von Sonnenfels, a prominent Viennese writer, reformer and professor. The nickname ‘Pastoral’ was added by the Hamburg publisher August Cranz in 1838 and suits the sonata’s gentle, rustic character; it is often heard as a forerunner of the Pastoral Symphony, which evokes country life on a larger scale.
parts: A tranquil movement over a persistent pedal bass.
A walking-bass march that Beethoven reportedly loved to play.
A humorous scherzo built on repeated single notes.
A rocking, bagpipe-like rondo with a brilliant coda.
facts: The nickname ‘Pastoral’ was added by the publisher Cranz in 1838.
Czerny recalled Beethoven often playing the Andante for his own pleasure.
The dedicatee, Joseph von Sonnenfels, was a leading figure of the Viennese Enlightenment.

33.about: Seven short, characterful pieces. Beethoven called them ‘Bagatelles’ — trifles — but each is carefully crafted, and together they cover a wide range of moods, from graceful, songful pieces to boisterous scherzos full of rhythmic jokes and sudden accents. They were an early example of a genre that Beethoven made his own, and they gave him a place to try out ideas in miniature.
33.ctx: The manuscript is dated 1782, when Beethoven was only eleven; the date is probably a mistake, though some of the pieces may indeed go back to his Bonn years. The set was assembled in 1801–02, while he was also working on the Op. 31 sonatas and the Second Symphony, and published in 1803. Their brevity and variety anticipate the Romantic character pieces of Schubert, Mendelssohn and Schumann.
facts: The title ‘Bagatelle’ means ‘trifle’.
Some pieces may date from Beethoven’s Bonn years.
Henle rates the pieces between levels 4 and 7.

34.about: Six variations on an original theme in F major. Instead of keeping to the home key, Beethoven sends the first five variations down through a chain of thirds — D major, B-flat, G, E-flat and C minor — each with its own tempo, metre and character, including a minuet and a march. The sixth returns to F, and an ornate coda brings back the theme. The result is less a set of decorations than a series of transformations.
34.ctx: In October 1802 Beethoven offered this set and the Op. 35 variations to Breitkopf & Härtel, stressing that both were written in a ‘quite new manner’, unlike anything he had done before. They belong to the year of his resolve to take a ‘new path’ in his music, and of the Heiligenstadt Testament. The set was published in 1803 with a dedication to Princess Barbara Odescalchi, his former pupil, who had also received the Sonata Op. 7 and the First Piano Concerto.
parts: A cheerful variation leading to a long, ornamented coda.
facts: Each variation is in a different key.
Beethoven described it as written in a new style.
Henle rates it level 7 (ABRSM ARSM).

35.about: A large set of fifteen variations and a fugue that begins, unusually, with the bass line alone, gradually building up the texture in two, three and four parts before the full theme appears. The variations range widely in character, from brilliant and witty to a sombre minor-key variation and a spacious, ornate Largo. The work ends with a powerful fugue built on the opening bass, followed by a final return of the theme in grand style.
35.ctx: The theme was a favourite of Beethoven’s: it appears in a set of contredanses, in the finale of his ballet The Creatures of Prometheus and, most famously, in the finale of the Eroica Symphony, where he repeated the idea of starting from the bare bass. Composed in 1802, the set was offered to Breitkopf & Härtel alongside Op. 34 as works in a ‘quite new manner’, and was published in 1803 with a dedication to Count Moritz von Lichnowsky. It is sometimes called the ‘Eroica Variations’.
facts: Its theme appears in the Eroica Symphony.
Beethoven described them as written in a ‘quite new manner’.
Henle rates it level 8 (ABRSM FRSM).

36.prem: 5 April 1803, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
36.about: The Second Symphony expands the scale of the First. Its long slow introduction includes a powerful D-minor outburst that seems to anticipate the Ninth Symphony, before an energetic Allegro con brio full of contrasts. The Larghetto is one of Beethoven’s most beautiful slow movements, a warm, flowing melody passed between strings and winds. The third movement is the first in his symphonies to be titled Scherzo, playful and full of sudden dynamic contrasts, and the finale is witty and explosive, opening with a hiccup-like motif and building to an extended coda.
36.ctx: Beethoven finished the symphony in 1802 at Heiligenstadt, where that autumn he wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament, a despairing letter to his brothers about his growing deafness. Yet the music’s high spirits show no trace of that crisis. It was premiered on 5 April 1803 at the Theater an der Wien, alongside the Third Piano Concerto and the oratorio Christ on the Mount of Olives, and was dedicated to Prince Karl von Lichnowsky. Some critics found it bizarre and noisy; one famously compared it to a wounded dragon that refuses to die and goes on thrashing about in the finale.
parts: A spacious introduction and a vigorous, surging Allegro.
A long, flowing and lyrical slow movement.
A playful scherzo with sudden dynamic contrasts.
A witty, explosive finale with an extended coda.
36.sc: 2 flutes, 2 oboes, 2 clarinets, 2 bassoons, 2 horns, 2 trumpets, timpani, strings
facts: A critic compared the finale to a ‘hideously writhing, wounded dragon’.
Completed in Heiligenstadt, the same autumn as the Heiligenstadt Testament.
It is the first of his symphonies with a movement called Scherzo.

37.prem: 5 April 1803, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
37.about: A dramatic concerto in C minor that owes something to Mozart’s Concerto No. 24 in the same key. The first movement’s theme is stated quietly by the strings before the full orchestra takes it up, and the piano enters with dramatic rushing scales. After the cadenza comes a quiet, mysterious coda in which the timpani echo the main theme. The Largo moves to the remote key of E major, creating a luminous stillness, and the rondo finale, with its energetic, syncopated theme, ends with a joyful switch to C major.
37.ctx: The concerto was premiered on 5 April 1803 at the Theater an der Wien, in the same concert as the Second Symphony. The piano part was not yet fully written out: Ignaz von Seyfried, who turned the pages, recalled nearly blank sheets with only a few scribbled signs, while Beethoven played largely from memory and nodded when he needed a turn. The concerto was published in 1804 with a dedication to Prince Louis Ferdinand of Prussia, a gifted pianist and composer who died in battle in 1806. The cadenza Beethoven wrote for the first movement in 1809 is still widely played.
parts: A stern, martial opening with a dramatic cadenza.
A restless rondo that turns to C major for a brilliant coda.
37.sc: Piano, 2 flutes, 2 oboes, 2 clarinets, 2 bassoons, 2 horns, 2 trumpets, timpani, strings
facts: Beethoven played from mostly blank pages at the premiere.
The dedicatee, Prince Louis Ferdinand, was himself a composer.
Its slow movement is in the distant key of E major.

40.about: A calm, dignified romance in G major for violin and orchestra. The violin opens alone with a hymn-like melody in double stops, answered by the orchestra, and this dialogue shapes the whole piece. Two contrasting episodes bring warmer, more restless moods before the serene main theme returns and the work closes quietly. Like its companion in F, it is a lyrical miniature that gives the soloist song rather than display.
40.ctx: Composed around 1801–02 and published in 1803, the Romance in G appeared before the Romance in F and so received the lower opus number, though it was written later. Both pieces may be by-products of Beethoven’s interest in the violin concerto, a form he had attempted in an unfinished concerto in C from his early years and would finally master in 1806. They remain popular with violinists as concert pieces and encores.
facts: The violin opens alone with double stops.
It was published before the Romance Op. 50.
It is in G major.

43.about: Beethoven’s only full-length ballet. In it the Titan Prometheus brings two statues to life and leads them to Parnassus, where Apollo, the Muses and other gods teach them music, dance and the arts. An energetic overture, still often played on its own, is followed by a series of dance numbers, including a rare solo for harp and an obbligato for basset horn. The finale’s buoyant contredanse theme became one of Beethoven’s favourite ideas, later used in the Eroica Variations and the finale of the Eroica Symphony.
43.ctx: The ballet was created with the choreographer Salvatore Viganò and premiered at the Burgtheater on 28 March 1801. It was a success, with 23 performances over the next two seasons — Beethoven’s first major triumph in the theatre. The piano arrangement was published in 1801 with a dedication to Princess Christiane von Lichnowsky, wife of his patron Prince Karl. The Promethean theme of enlightenment through the arts appealed strongly to Beethoven, who returned to it in the Eroica.
parts: A brilliant overture with a slow introduction.
Prometheus brings his statues to life.
The statues are educated in the arts; the finale theme was later used in the Eroica.
43.sc: Orchestra with harp and basset horn
facts: Its finale theme reappears in the Eroica Symphony.
It uses a harp, rare in Beethoven’s music.
It had 23 performances in its first two years.

46.about: A long, lyrical love song on a poem by Friedrich von Matthisson, in which the lover sees and hears the name ‘Adelaide’ everywhere in nature — in the blossoms, the waves, the evening breeze and the nightingale’s song. Beethoven sets it almost as a small concert aria in two parts: a broad, tender Larghetto followed by a more passionate Allegro molto, with a flowing piano accompaniment that paints the images of the poem. It remains one of the best-loved songs of the classical era.
46.ctx: Composed in 1794–95, soon after Beethoven settled in Vienna, and published in 1797 by Artaria, ‘Adelaide’ was one of his most popular songs during his lifetime. He dedicated it to the poet, and when he sent Matthisson a copy in 1800 he wrote modestly that he feared the poet might not like it. Matthisson later acknowledged that no other composer had set his poem so well.
facts: It was one of Beethoven’s most popular songs.
It was dedicated to the poet Matthisson.
Liszt made a famous piano transcription of it.

47.about: A concerto-like sonata of great virtuosity and scale. A slow introduction, beginning with the violin alone in rich double stops, leads to a fiery, dramatic Presto in A minor. The middle movement is a set of four elaborate variations on a lyrical theme in F major, closing with a serene coda. The finale, a whirling tarantella in 6/8, was originally written for the Sonata Op. 30 No. 1. On the title page Beethoven described the work as written ‘in a very concertante style, almost like a concerto’.
47.ctx: Beethoven wrote the sonata for the violinist George Bridgetower, a virtuoso of African and European descent, who premiered it with Beethoven at the Augarten on 24 May 1803. It was finished so late that Bridgetower had to read part of it from Beethoven’s manuscript. After a quarrel, reportedly over a woman, Beethoven withdrew his intended dedication and inscribed it instead to the French violinist Rodolphe Kreutzer, who reportedly never played it and found it unintelligible. The sonata later inspired Tolstoy’s novella The Kreutzer Sonata, which in turn inspired Janáček’s First String Quartet.
parts: A slow, searching introduction leads to a fiery, virtuosic Presto.
Four virtuosic variations and a serene coda.
facts: Bridgetower sight-read parts of it at the premiere.
Kreutzer reportedly never played it.
Tolstoy and Janáček both created works named after it.

50.about: A sweet, songful romance in F major for violin and orchestra. The violin sings a gently flowing melody, which the orchestra echoes, and returns to it after two contrasting episodes, the second turning briefly to the minor. The writing is lyrical rather than virtuosic, and the piece’s warmth and simplicity have made it one of Beethoven’s most popular short works.
50.ctx: Although numbered second, the Romance in F was written around 1798, before the Romance in G, Op. 40; it was simply published later, in 1805. Both romances may have been conceived as studies for a violin concerto, a genre Beethoven would not complete until 1806. The F-major Romance is often played as an encore and appears frequently in arrangements for other instruments.
facts: It was written before the Romance Op. 40.
It is one of Beethoven’s most popular short works.
It is often performed as an encore.

53.about: The ‘Waldstein’ is a landmark of Beethoven’s heroic style, full of energy and light. It opens with pulsing repeated chords in the bass, pianissimo, that gradually build to a brilliant climax as the harmony moves quickly through distant keys; a chorale-like second theme in E major provides calm contrast. The second movement, marked Introduzione: Adagio molto, is a short, brooding bridge leading straight into the finale. The Rondo begins with a radiant, bell-like theme over shimmering trills and long pedals, builds to a grand climax and ends with a dazzling Prestissimo coda that includes octave glissandos. Its orchestral textures exploit the wider range of the pianos of the day.
53.ctx: The sonata was dedicated to Count Ferdinand von Waldstein, Beethoven’s early patron in Bonn, who had sent him to Vienna with the wish that he would receive ‘the spirit of Mozart from the hands of Haydn’. Beethoven wrote it in 1803–04, soon after receiving a new piano from the French maker Érard with a wider range and a different sound. The original slow movement was a longer Andante; when a friend remarked that it made the sonata too long, Beethoven replaced it with the short Introduzione and published the Andante separately as the ‘Andante favori’, WoO 57.
parts: Pulsing chords and sudden key shifts in a wide-ranging sonata form.
A short, mysterious bridge leading directly into the finale.
A radiant, bell-like theme over trills, ending in a brilliant coda.
facts: The original slow movement became the ‘Andante favori’, WoO 57.

54.about: An enigmatic two-movement sonata overshadowed by its neighbours, the ‘Waldstein’ and the ‘Appassionata’. The first movement, In tempo d’un menuetto, alternates a courtly minuet with blunt, stomping octave passages, as if two characters were arguing. The second, Allegretto, is a relentless two-part invention in perpetual motion that accelerates into a Più allegro coda. Its concentration and experimental character make it a fascinating, if puzzling, work, and pianists such as Sviatoslav Richter have championed it.
54.ctx: Composed in 1804, the year of the Triple Concerto and the beginning of the ‘Appassionata’, the sonata was published in 1806 without a dedication. Its compact size and unusual structure contrast sharply with the grand sonatas around it, and commentators have long been divided: some find it strange, others admire its subtlety. Its experiments with contrast and continuous motion point towards the concentration of Beethoven’s later style.
parts: A courtly minuet interrupted by rough, stomping octaves.

facts: It is sandwiched between the Waldstein and Appassionata sonatas.

55.prem: Private 1804 at Prince Lobkowitz’s; public 7 April 1805, Theater an der Wien
55.about: The ‘Eroica’ redefined the symphony. Its first movement, nearly as long as an entire Haydn symphony, is launched by two sharp E-flat chords; the simple arpeggio theme is soon unsettled by a strange C-sharp in the cellos, and the movement unfolds as a drama of conflict, with harsh, syncopated dissonances and a new theme in E minor in the development. Famously, a horn enters with the main theme just before the recapitulation, apparently too early. The second movement is a solemn funeral march in C minor with a fugal climax, the scherzo a whispering, driving movement with a trio for three horns, and the finale a set of variations on a theme from The Creatures of Prometheus, building to a triumphant coda.
55.ctx: Beethoven originally planned to name the symphony after Napoleon Bonaparte, whom he admired as a champion of revolutionary ideals. According to Ferdinand Ries, when Beethoven heard in May 1804 that Napoleon had declared himself emperor, he flew into a rage and tore the title page in two; a surviving copy shows the words ‘intitolata Bonaparte’ scratched out so violently that the paper is torn. The published title reads ‘Sinfonia eroica, composed to celebrate the memory of a great man’. After private performances at the palace of Prince Lobkowitz, who bought exclusive rights to it for a time and received the dedication, it was first heard publicly on 7 April 1805 at the Theater an der Wien.
parts: Two sharp chords launch a vast, conflicted drama.
A funeral march with a noble major-key middle section and a fugal climax.
A whispering, driving scherzo with a trio for three horns.
Variations on a theme from The Creatures of Prometheus, ending in triumph.

56.prem: Probably 1804, private; public May 1808, Augarten, Vienna
56.about: A unique concerto for piano trio — piano, violin and cello — and orchestra. The work is genial and warm rather than dramatic, and the cello, playing high in its range, usually introduces each new theme before the violin and piano take it up. The broad first movement has the soloists trading ideas in a sunny, spacious dialogue. The Largo is short and songful, led again by the cello, and runs straight into the finale, a lively rondo alla polacca with a contrasting minor-key episode. The unusual scoring blends chamber-music intimacy with orchestral grandeur.
56.ctx: Beethoven composed the Triple Concerto in 1803–04, alongside the Eroica and the ‘Waldstein’. According to Schindler, the relatively modest piano part was written for his teenage pupil Archduke Rudolph, while the demanding cello part may have been intended for the renowned cellist Anton Kraft. Probably first played privately at Prince Lobkowitz’s palace, it was published in 1807 with a dedication to Lobkowitz and first heard publicly in May 1808 at the Augarten. Long overshadowed by Beethoven’s other concertos, it is now a favourite showcase for established piano trios.

57.about: The ‘Appassionata’ is one of the most intense works in the piano repertoire. The first movement opens with whispered arpeggios in unison and ominous four-note knocks that recall the Fifth Symphony, building to explosive climaxes; its lyrical second theme, derived from the first, offers only brief relief. The second movement is a set of serene variations on a chorale-like theme in D-flat major, broken off by a crashing diminished-seventh chord that leads straight into the finale. This Allegro ma non troppo is a relentless, whirling perpetual motion that ends in a ferocious Presto coda. Its demands on power and stamina make it a cornerstone of the virtuoso repertoire.
57.ctx: Composed in 1804–05 and published in 1807, the sonata was dedicated to Count Franz von Brunsvik, a close friend of Beethoven and brother of Therese and Josephine Brunsvik. The nickname ‘Appassionata’ was added by the Hamburg publisher Cranz in 1838. Ferdinand Ries recalled that Beethoven worked out the finale during a long country walk, humming and howling to himself. According to Czerny, Beethoven considered it his greatest sonata until he wrote the Hammerklavier, and Lenin is said to have admired it above all other music.

58.prem: March 1807, Palais Lobkowitz (private); 22 December 1808, Theater an der Wien (public)
58.about: A lyrical, poetic concerto that begins, unusually, with the solo piano quietly stating the theme before the orchestra answers in the distant key of B major. Throughout the first movement the piano leads rather than follows, in an intimate dialogue with the orchestra. The short slow movement sets stern unison strings against a soft, pleading piano that gradually calms them — often compared to Orpheus taming the Furies. The finale bursts in with rhythmic energy, beginning in the ‘wrong’ key of C major, and brings in the trumpets and timpani for the first time in the work.
58.ctx: Beethoven composed the concerto in 1805–06, alongside the Fourth Symphony and the Violin Concerto. After a private performance at Prince Lobkowitz’s palace in March 1807, he gave the public premiere on 22 December 1808 at the Theater an der Wien — his last appearance as soloist in a concerto. The work was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph. Opening a concerto with the soloist alone was almost unprecedented, and the work’s lyricism later influenced Brahms. Neglected after Beethoven’s death, it was revived by Mendelssohn in 1836.
parts: The piano opens alone, gently; the orchestra replies in B major.

60.about: The Fourth Symphony emerges from a shadowy introduction into brilliant light. The Adagio opening, in B-flat minor, is hushed and harmonically wandering, until a sudden crescendo launches the joyous Allegro vivace. The slow movement, in E-flat major, is serene and singing, underpinned by a persistent dotted rhythm, with a famous clarinet solo. The third movement is a lively scherzo whose trio is heard twice, a plan Beethoven reused in the Seventh Symphony. The finale is a whirlwind of rapid notes, including a notoriously difficult bassoon solo, and ends with a humorous slowdown before the final dash.
60.ctx: Beethoven wrote the symphony in the summer of 1806 while staying with Prince Lichnowsky at his castle in Silesia, where he met Count Franz von Oppersdorff, who commissioned it and received the dedication. It was first performed privately in March 1807 at Prince Lobkowitz’s palace. Scored for a small orchestra with a single flute, it is often overshadowed by the Eroica and the Fifth — Schumann is said to have called it ‘a slender Greek maiden between two Norse giants’. Not everyone was charmed: Weber, in a satirical review, mocked its slow introduction for having only three or four notes per quarter of an hour.
parts: A hushed, uncertain introduction erupts into a joyous Allegro.
A gentle, singing movement over a steady dotted pulse.
A lively scherzo whose trio is heard twice.

61.prem: 23 December 1806, Theater an der Wien (Franz Clement, soloist)
61.about: One of the greatest violin concertos, serene and lyrical rather than showy. It opens with four quiet timpani strokes, a motif that runs through the first movement in the strings and winds. After a leisurely orchestral introduction, the violin enters with a rising line and sings mostly high, lyrical melodies. The Larghetto is a calm set of variations in which the violin decorates a simple theme, and a short cadenza leads into the rondo, a lively, dancing movement with hunting-horn calls.
61.ctx: Beethoven wrote the concerto in 1806 for the violinist Franz Clement, who premiered it on 23 December at the Theater an der Wien, reportedly almost at sight; in the same concert Clement played a showpiece of his own with the violin held upside down. The concerto made little impression at first and was rarely heard until the 12-year-old Joseph Joachim played it in London under Mendelssohn in 1844. Beethoven dedicated it to his childhood friend Stephan von Breuning, and also arranged it as a piano concerto (Op. 61a), with a cadenza that features the timpani.

Gentle variations leading straight into the finale.
A dance-like rondo with hunting-horn flavour.

62.about: A dark, dramatic overture that portrays the Roman general Coriolanus, who, banished from Rome, leads an enemy army against his own city, only to be moved to spare it by his mother’s pleas. Beethoven captures the conflict in two sharply contrasted ideas: a restless, forceful C-minor theme for the proud, defiant hero, and a tender, pleading melody for his mother. The music never resolves in triumph, ending instead with a quiet, dying fall as the hero’s resolve disintegrates.
62.ctx: Beethoven wrote the overture in 1807 for Heinrich Joseph von Collin’s tragedy Coriolan — not Shakespeare’s play, as is often assumed. Collin’s drama had by then largely left the stage, and the overture was first heard at a private concert at Prince Lobkowitz’s palace in March 1807; it may have been used at a single later performance of the play. Published in 1808 with a dedication to Collin, it quickly became a concert piece in its own right.

facts: It was written for Collin’s play, not Shakespeare’s.

67.prem: 22 December 1808, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
67.about: Its four-note motif — short-short-short-long — is perhaps the most famous opening in music, and it permeates the whole symphony, which moves from C-minor struggle to C-major triumph. The first movement is concise and relentless, built almost entirely from the motif, with a brief, plaintive oboe cadenza in the recapitulation. The Andante con moto is a set of double variations alternating a gentle theme with a martial fanfare. The spectral scherzo, with its gruff, fugal trio for cellos and basses, fades into a suspenseful passage over a timpani pedal that bursts without a break into the blazing finale, where piccolo, contrabassoon and trombones join the orchestra for the first time in a Beethoven symphony.
67.ctx: The symphony was premiered on 22 December 1808 at the Theater an der Wien, in a four-hour concert in an unheated hall that also included the Pastoral Symphony, the Fourth Piano Concerto, the Choral Fantasy, parts of the Mass in C and the aria ‘Ah! perfido’; the orchestra was under-rehearsed and the audience cold and tired. E.T.A. Hoffmann’s 1810 review hailed it as a masterpiece of Romanticism. The idea that the opening depicts ‘fate knocking at the door’ comes from Schindler, whose reports are unreliable. During the Second World War the motif became an Allied symbol of victory, because its rhythm matches the Morse code for V.

68.prem: 22 December 1808, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
68.about: Beethoven’s nature symphony, in five movements with descriptive titles. The first depicts the awakening of cheerful feelings on arriving in the countryside, with gentle, repeated patterns. The second, a scene by the brook, has murmuring strings and ends with a cadenza of birdsong for nightingale (flute), quail (oboe) and cuckoo (clarinet). The third is a merry gathering of country folk, complete with a clumsy village band, which is cut short by a thunderstorm that brings in the timpani and piccolo for the first time. The finale, following without a break, is the shepherd’s song of thanksgiving after the storm, built on a yodel-like theme.
68.ctx: Beethoven loved long walks in the countryside around Vienna, often composed outdoors and sketched birdsong in his notebooks. He described the symphony as ‘more the expression of feeling than painting’, to avoid being thought of as writing mere imitation. It was premiered on 22 December 1808 in the same concert as the Fifth Symphony, and the two works share their dedication to Prince Lobkowitz and Count Razumovsky. The symphony helped inspire later programme music, from Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique to Liszt’s symphonic poems, and reached a new audience through Disney’s Fantasia (1940).

69.about: A landmark of the cello repertoire, in which cello and piano are fully equal partners. It opens with the cello alone singing a noble theme, which the piano then completes, and the whole spacious first movement is built on this kind of balanced exchange. A syncopated, off-balance scherzo in A minor follows. A brief Adagio cantabile, only a few bars long, then serves as an introduction to the joyful, sunlit finale.
69.ctx: Composed in 1807–08, the same years as the Fifth and Sixth Symphonies, the sonata was dedicated to Baron Ignaz von Gleichenstein, a close friend who helped Beethoven with his business affairs and was himself an amateur cellist. On Gleichenstein’s copy Beethoven wrote ‘Inter lacrimas et luctum’ (amid tears and sorrow), perhaps reflecting the hardships of 1809, when French troops occupied Vienna. It is the most frequently played of his five cello sonatas.

72.prem: 20 November 1805 (as Leonore), Theater an der Wien; final version 23 May 1814, Kärntnertortheater
72.about: Beethoven’s only opera tells of Leonore, who disguises herself as a young man, Fidelio, and takes work at a prison to rescue her husband Florestan, a political prisoner held in secret by the tyrannical governor Pizarro. It begins almost as a domestic comedy but darkens and deepens as it moves to Florestan’s dungeon, where Leonore saves him at the last moment and a trumpet call announces the arrival of the minister. Highlights include the hushed Prisoners’ Chorus, Leonore’s great aria ‘Abscheulicher!’ and Florestan’s dungeon scene, and the opera ends with a jubilant celebration of married love, freedom and justice.
72.ctx: The first version, titled Leonore, was premiered on 20 November 1805, a week after Napoleon’s troops occupied Vienna; the audience was made up largely of French officers, and it was a failure. Beethoven shortened it for a revival in 1806, then revised it thoroughly, with a reworked libretto by Georg Friedrich Treitschke, for the final version, triumphantly premiered on 23 May 1814 at the Kärntnertortheater. He wrote four overtures for the opera: the three Leonore overtures and the Fidelio overture. He reportedly said that of all his works it had cost him the worst birth pangs.

73.about: Beethoven’s last and grandest piano concerto opens with the piano sweeping through flourishes over three massive orchestral chords before the main theme appears. The first movement is on a grand, military scale, and instead of leaving room for a cadenza Beethoven wrote into the score that the pianist should not add one but go straight on. The Adagio un poco mosso is a serene hymn in B major for muted strings, over which the piano enters with a delicate, ornamented line. At its end the piano quietly previews the finale’s theme before bursting into the jubilant rondo, with its dancing, syncopated theme.
73.ctx: Composed in 1809, while Napoleon’s army besieged and occupied Vienna, the concerto was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph, Beethoven’s pupil and patron. By then Beethoven was too deaf to perform it himself: it was premiered on 28 November 1811 at the Leipzig Gewandhaus, with Friedrich Schneider as soloist, and Carl Czerny gave the Vienna premiere in 1812. The nickname ‘Emperor’ was not Beethoven’s and was probably coined by the English publisher Johann Baptist Cramer. It was the last concerto Beethoven completed; a sixth piano concerto, begun in 1815, was abandoned.

74.about: A warm, expansive quartet in E-flat major, nicknamed ‘Harp’ after the pizzicato arpeggios passed between the instruments in the first movement. After a hushed slow introduction, the Allegro builds to a brilliant climax in which the first violin races above the plucked accompaniment. The Adagio ma non troppo is a deeply lyrical song, and the scherzo, a Presto in C minor, is driving and relentless, recalling the Fifth Symphony. The finale is a set of six variations on a simple theme, rounded off by a quick, abrupt coda.
74.ctx: Beethoven wrote the quartet in 1809, the year Napoleon’s army bombarded and occupied Vienna, alongside the ‘Emperor’ Concerto and the ‘Les Adieux’ Sonata. It was his first quartet since the three ‘Razumovsky’ Quartets of 1806, and it is more relaxed and lyrical than they are. The nickname ‘Harp’ was not his. Published in 1810 by Breitkopf & Härtel, it was dedicated to Prince Lobkowitz, one of his most loyal patrons, who had also commissioned the Op. 18 quartets.

78.about: A short, affectionate two-movement sonata in the rare key of F-sharp major. A four-bar Adagio cantabile introduction leads to a warm, lyrical Allegro ma non troppo. The second movement, Allegro vivace, is playful and quick, with bright, rocking figures, off-beat accents and sudden turns that demand a light touch and precise rhythm. Its intimate tone suggests a private gift, and it has long been a favourite among pianists, despite its daunting six-sharp key signature.
78.ctx: Composed in 1809, the year of the ‘Emperor’ Concerto and ‘Les Adieux’, and published in 1810, the sonata was dedicated to Countess Therese von Brunsvik, one of Beethoven’s closest friends. Czerny reported that Beethoven was particularly fond of it and considered it better than the ‘Moonlight’ Sonata, which he felt received too much attention. Therese was once proposed as the ‘Immortal Beloved’ of Beethoven’s famous 1812 letter, though scholars now favour other candidates, including her sister Josephine.

79.about: A light, compact sonata described on its first edition as a ‘sonatine’. The first movement, Presto alla tedesca, is a lively German dance in which the hands cross to toss a cuckoo-like figure back and forth. The Andante in G minor is a gently swaying barcarolle, its melody in thirds evoking a Venetian gondola song. The brief Vivace finale is cheerful and lighthearted. Its easy charm makes it one of the most approachable of Beethoven’s mature sonatas.
79.ctx: Composed in 1809 and published in 1810 without a dedication, the sonata was written alongside the ‘Emperor’ Concerto and the ‘Harp’ Quartet. That year Napoleon’s army bombarded Vienna, and Beethoven sheltered in his brother’s cellar with pillows over his ears to protect what remained of his hearing. The nickname ‘Cuckoo’ refers to the first movement’s cuckoo-call figures. The sonata is often taught to intermediate students as a first step towards the larger sonatas.

80.ded: King Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria
80.prem: 22 December 1808, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
80.about: A unique work for piano, orchestra and chorus. It begins with a long, improvisatory piano solo — which Beethoven actually improvised at the premiere — before the orchestra enters and the piano introduces a simple, folk-like theme. A series of variations passes the tune through solo instruments and the full orchestra, before vocal soloists and chorus take it up to a poem praising the power of music. The theme anticipates the ‘Ode to Joy’ of the Ninth Symphony, and the work is often heard as a study for it.
80.ctx: Beethoven wrote the Choral Fantasy as a rousing finale for his marathon concert of 22 December 1808, which also premiered the Fifth and Sixth Symphonies and the Fourth Piano Concerto. Hastily prepared, the performance broke down and had to be restarted. The text, probably by Christoph Kuffner, was written to fit music already composed, and the theme comes from Beethoven’s earlier song ‘Gegenliebe’. It was published in 1811 with a dedication to King Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria. Beethoven later described the finale of the Ninth Symphony as being in the same style as the Choral Fantasy, but on a much larger scale.

84.about: A dramatic overture depicting the struggle and triumph of Count Egmont, a nobleman of the Netherlands executed for resisting Spanish oppression. It opens with a sombre, heavy introduction in F minor, whose slow sarabande-like rhythms suggest the weight of Spanish rule. The Allegro that follows is tense and driven, and after a sudden silence that represents Egmont’s execution, the music bursts into F major for a jubilant coda — the ‘Victory Symphony’ that also ends Goethe’s play.
84.ctx: The overture is part of the incidental music Beethoven wrote in 1809–10 for a Vienna revival of Goethe’s play Egmont, first performed with his music on 15 June 1810 at the Burgtheater. Beethoven revered Goethe and took on the commission gladly, and the play’s themes of freedom and heroic sacrifice clearly spoke to him. The two men met in 1812 at the spa town of Teplitz, though their personalities did not mix easily. The overture soon became a concert piece in its own right and a symbol of resistance to oppression.

90.about: A two-movement sonata in E minor with German tempo markings instead of the usual Italian, the first of Beethoven’s sonatas to use them. The first movement is compact, agitated and emotional, with sudden changes of mood. The second is a long, flowing rondo in E major whose endlessly singing main theme, marked to be played ‘very singingly’, returns many times with subtle changes and is often compared to Schubert. Its lyrical warmth answers the first movement’s turbulence, and the sonata stands at the threshold between Beethoven’s middle and late styles.
90.ctx: Composed in 1814 and published in 1815 by Steiner, the sonata was dedicated to Count Moritz von Lichnowsky, brother of Beethoven’s early patron Prince Karl. According to Schindler, Beethoven told the count that the two movements represented ‘a struggle between head and heart’ and ‘conversation with the beloved’, alluding to the count’s romance with the singer Josepha Stummer, whom he later married. It was written during the Congress of Vienna, when Europe’s rulers and diplomats gathered in the city and Beethoven enjoyed the greatest public fame of his life.

92.about: A symphony driven by rhythm. After a grand, spacious introduction, the first movement dances in a lilting dotted rhythm. The Allegretto, built on a steady, processional pattern (long-short-short-long-long) beneath a haunting melody, was encored at the premiere and has remained one of Beethoven’s most popular movements, often performed on its own and used in many films. The Presto is an exhilarating scherzo with a hymn-like trio that is heard twice, and the finale is a frenzied, spinning dance. Wagner famously called the symphony ‘the apotheosis of the dance’.
92.ctx: The symphony was premiered on 8 December 1813 in the hall of the University of Vienna, conducted by Beethoven, at a charity concert for soldiers wounded at the Battle of Hanau that also introduced Wellington’s Victory. The orchestra included such distinguished musicians as Spohr, Salieri, Hummel and Meyerbeer, and the Allegretto had to be repeated. It became one of Beethoven’s greatest public successes and was given several more times in the following months. Some critics found its rhythmic insistence excessive, and there is a doubtful story that Weber declared Beethoven ‘ripe for the madhouse’. It was dedicated to Count Moritz von Fries.

A hypnotic processional built on a repeated long-short-short rhythm.

93.about: One of Beethoven’s most compact and witty symphonies, playing affectionately with classical forms. The first movement starts at full speed with no introduction, its main theme stated forte at once. The Allegretto scherzando ticks steadily in the winds beneath a playful string melody, and the third movement is a deliberately old-fashioned minuet with a trio for horns and clarinet. The finale is full of surprises, including a startling C-sharp that eventually wrenches the music into F-sharp minor before it returns to F major, and a long coda that seems to end several times before the final chords.
93.ctx: Beethoven composed the symphony in 1812, partly in Linz, where he was visiting his brother Johann, and called it his ‘little symphony in F’. It was premiered on 27 February 1814 in the Redoutensaal in Vienna, on a programme that also included the more popular Seventh; when audiences preferred the Seventh, Beethoven reportedly said it was because the Eighth was ‘so much better’. The ticking second movement was long linked to Johann Nepomuk Maelzel’s metronome through a canon Beethoven supposedly wrote for him, but the canon is now thought to be a forgery by Schindler.
parts: A compact, genial movement that starts at full speed.
A deliberately old-fashioned minuet with a horn-and-clarinet trio.

95.about: Beethoven’s most compressed and volatile quartet, which he titled ‘Quartetto serioso’. Its four movements are short and full of abrupt contrasts: a fierce, explosive opening Allegro con brio, a searching Allegretto with a nervous fugato, a tense scherzo driven by dotted rhythms, and a finale whose agitation suddenly gives way to a brief, almost comic coda in F major. Every movement is pared down to the essentials, with sudden silences and changes of key.
95.ctx: Composed in 1810, the quartet was not published until 1816, and Beethoven wrote to the English conductor George Smart that it was intended ‘for a small circle of connoisseurs’ and never to be performed in public. It was dedicated to Nikolaus Zmeskall, an official at the Hungarian court chancellery, a keen amateur cellist and one of Beethoven’s oldest friends in Vienna. Its concentrated, experimental style looks forward to the late quartets.

96.prem: 29 December 1812, Vienna (Pierre Rode, violin; Archduke Rudolph, piano)
96.about: Beethoven’s last violin sonata is intimate and reflective. The first movement opens with a gentle trill, and its lyrical themes unfold naturally in a relaxed dialogue between the instruments. The Adagio espressivo is hymn-like and leads without a break into a brief, playful scherzo in G minor with a waltz-like trio. The finale is a set of variations on a folk-like tune that takes surprising turns, including an introspective Adagio and a fugato, before a brisk close.
96.ctx: Beethoven wrote the sonata in 1812 for the French violinist Pierre Rode, whose sweet, gentle style shaped the finale in particular; Beethoven explained that he had to take Rode’s playing into account. Rode premiered it on 29 December 1812 with Archduke Rudolph, Beethoven’s pupil and patron and the work’s dedicatee, at the piano. Beethoven revised it before publication in 1816. The sonata dates from the same year as his famous letter to the ‘Immortal Beloved’.

97.about: Beethoven’s grandest piano trio. The first movement opens with a broad, noble theme on the piano, taken up by the strings, and unfolds on a spacious, symphonic scale. The scherzo is playful, with a trio that alternates a creeping chromatic fugato with a boisterous waltz. The Andante cantabile is a set of serene variations on a hymn-like theme, and it leads without a break into the finale, a lively rondo ending in a brilliant Presto.
97.ctx: Composed in 1811 and published in 1816, the trio was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph, Beethoven’s pupil and patron, who also gave it its nickname. Beethoven played the piano part at the premiere on 11 April 1814; Louis Spohr, who heard him rehearse it, recorded that his deafness made his playing painfully unreliable, too loud in the forte passages and barely audible in the soft ones. It was one of his last public appearances as a pianist.

98.about: Often called the first true song cycle: six songs on poems by Alois Jeitteles, in which a lover, far from his beloved, sends his longing to her through nature — the hills, the clouds, the breezes, the brook and the birds. The songs are linked by piano transitions and flow without a break, and at the end the melody of the first song returns, bringing the cycle full circle. Beethoven gives the voice simple, heartfelt melodies, while the piano deepens the mood and ties the whole together.
98.ctx: Composed in 1816 and published the same year with a dedication to Prince Lobkowitz, one of Beethoven’s most loyal patrons, the cycle was written at a time when Beethoven was composing relatively little. Its idea of a continuous chain of songs that returns at the end to its beginning strongly influenced later song cycles, notably those of Schubert and Schumann. Some have heard in its theme of a distant beloved an echo of Beethoven’s own unfulfilled longing.

101.about: The first of the late sonatas, deeply lyrical and inward. The first movement begins with a dreamy melody that seems to start mid-thought, avoiding a firm tonic chord, and is marked ‘Etwas lebhaft und mit der innigsten Empfindung’ (somewhat lively, with the most heartfelt feeling). A vigorous march of dotted rhythms follows, with a delicate canonic trio. A short, yearning Adagio recalls the opening theme before breaking into the finale, which contains a substantial fugue — a hallmark of Beethoven’s late style — and ends with a triumphant coda. The sonata’s continuous flow and cyclic recall anticipate the late quartets.
101.ctx: Composed in 1816 and published in 1817, the sonata marks the beginning of Beethoven’s late period, after several years of low productivity. It was the first in which he called the instrument by the German name ‘Hammerklavier’, reflecting his growing preference for German terms. It was dedicated to Baroness Dorothea von Ertmann, one of the finest interpreters of his piano music, whom he called his ‘Dorothea-Cäcilia’. Mendelssohn later passed on her story that when her child died, Beethoven comforted her by improvising at the piano for an hour.

106.about: Beethoven’s longest and most demanding sonata. The first movement opens with a mighty leap and grand chords, and its development includes a complex fugato. The scherzo is brusque and capricious, with a strange, shadowy trio and a sudden prestissimo outburst. The Adagio sostenuto in F-sharp minor is one of the longest slow movements Beethoven wrote, a profound meditation that can last nearly 20 minutes. The finale begins with a searching, improvisatory Largo that leads to a colossal, dissonant three-voice fugue ‘con alcune licenze’ (with some liberties), full of trills, leaps and harmonic clashes. The interval of a falling third links themes and keys across all four movements.
106.ctx: Composed in 1817–18, during Beethoven’s bitter legal battle for custody of his nephew Karl, the sonata was published in 1819 and dedicated to Archduke Rudolph. Beethoven told his publisher it would give pianists something to do when it was played fifty years later. For decades it was considered almost unplayable, until Liszt gave one of the first famous performances in Paris in 1836; Hans von Bülow and others later helped establish it in the concert hall. Beethoven’s metronome markings, especially the very fast tempo for the first movement, have been debated ever since.

109.about: An intimate late sonata in three movements, weighted towards its finale. The first alternates flowing figuration with slow, improvisatory Adagio interruptions, creating a sense of spontaneity. A fierce, concise Prestissimo in E minor follows. The heart of the work is the finale, a set of six variations on a hymn-like theme marked ‘Gesangvoll, mit innigster Empfindung’ (songful, with the most heartfelt feeling), which lasts longer than the first two movements together. The variations range from a lyrical waltz to a fugato and a final variation of trills and shimmering figuration, after which the theme returns in its simplest form, bringing a sense of peace.
109.ctx: Composed in 1820, while Beethoven was also working on the Missa Solemnis, and published by Schlesinger in Berlin in 1821, this was the first of his last three sonatas, written in quick succession. It was dedicated to Maximiliane Brentano, daughter of Antonie and Franz Brentano, close friends of Beethoven; he had written a short piano trio for her in 1812, when she was ten. Antonie Brentano is one of the leading candidates for Beethoven’s ‘Immortal Beloved’.

110.about: A deeply personal sonata that moves from quiet lyricism to triumph. The first movement is gentle and songful, with flowing arpeggios, and the scherzo is abrupt and humorous. The finale alternates a sorrowful ‘arioso dolente’ with a fugue: the lament returns, weaker, marked ‘ermattet, klagend’ (exhausted, lamenting), before the fugue rises again with its subject inverted, gathering strength and speed into a radiant close in A-flat major. This lament–fugue–lament–fugue design is unique in the sonata literature.
110.ctx: Composed in 1821–22 and published in 1822 without a dedication, the sonata was written alongside the Missa Solemnis and Op. 111; Beethoven dated the autograph 25 December 1821. He had been seriously ill with jaundice that year, and many hear the finale’s alternation of lament and fugue as a journey from exhaustion to recovery. The scherzo quotes two popular Viennese street songs, ‘Unsa Kätz häd Katz’ln ghabt’ (Our cat has had kittens) and ‘Ich bin lüderlich, du bist lüderlich’ (I’m a slob, you’re a slob). It is often considered the most personal of the last three sonatas.

111.about: Beethoven’s last piano sonata, in only two movements. The first is a fierce C-minor struggle: a dramatic introduction of diminished-seventh chords and double-dotted rhythms, recalling the French overture, leads to a fugal Allegro con brio ed appassionato. The second, the Arietta, is a set of variations on a simple, hymn-like theme in C major. Each variation subdivides the rhythm further — including a famous syncopated variation often compared to jazz or boogie-woogie — until the music dissolves into trills and high, luminous textures, leaving the struggles of the first movement far behind.
111.ctx: Composed in 1821–22 and published in 1823, the sonata was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph; the English edition was dedicated to Antonie Brentano. When asked why there was no third movement, Beethoven reportedly replied that he had not had time. It was the last of his thirty-two sonatas; though he lived another five years, he never returned to the genre. Thomas Mann devoted a famous passage of his novel Doctor Faustus to the Arietta, in which a lecturer explains why the sonata could have no third movement.

119.about: Eleven concise, whimsical and experimental pieces, some only a few bars long. They range from a graceful G-minor Allegretto and gentle, songful Andantes to brusque, humorous miniatures full of rhythmic surprises and abrupt endings. In their brevity and unpredictability they try out in miniature ideas that Beethoven developed on a larger scale in his late sonatas, and they make an excellent introduction to his late style.
119.ctx: Beethoven drew some of the pieces from earlier sketches, a few dating back to the 1790s, and wrote the last five in 1820 for a piano method compiled by Friedrich Starke. The complete set was published in 1823. His publisher Peters rejected the bagatelles as unworthy of his reputation, but Beethoven thought well of them. Their extreme concentration anticipates the miniatures of later composers, from Schumann to Webern.

120.about: One of the greatest sets of variations ever written. From a simple waltz by Anton Diabelli, Beethoven creates 33 variations of immense variety, ranging from parody and grotesque humour to profound meditation. Some take the waltz apart into its tiniest fragments; the first turns it into a pompous march, and another mockingly quotes Mozart. After a sequence of slow, inward variations in C minor, the work culminates in a vigorous double fugue and a graceful, transfigured minuet.
120.ctx: In 1819 the publisher and composer Anton Diabelli invited leading composers in Austria to write a single variation each on his waltz for a collective volume; among the contributors were Schubert and the 11-year-old Liszt. Beethoven instead began a set of his own, put it aside for the Missa Solemnis, and completed 33 variations in 1823. Variation 22 quotes Leporello’s grumbling aria ‘Notte e giorno faticar’ from Don Giovanni. The set was dedicated to Antonie Brentano.

123.about: One of the greatest settings of the Mass, a deeply personal work of vast scale and dramatic contrast. The Kyrie is broad and reverent, while the Gloria and Credo are jubilant and dramatic, each ending with an enormous fugue. In the Benedictus a solo violin descends like a blessing from above, and in the Agnus Dei the prayer for peace is interrupted by distant military drums and trumpets before the work closes with a final plea for inner and outer peace.
123.ctx: Beethoven began the Missa Solemnis in 1819 for the enthronement of his pupil Archduke Rudolph as Archbishop of Olmütz, but it was not finished until 1823, three years after the ceremony. He considered it his greatest work, and at the head of the Kyrie he wrote ‘Von Herzen – Möge es wieder – zu Herzen gehn!’ (From the heart – may it go again – to the heart!). The first complete performance was given in St Petersburg on 7 April 1824, organised by Prince Nikolai Galitzin; Vienna heard only three movements a month later, in the concert that premiered the Ninth Symphony.

125.ded: King Frederick William III of Prussia
125.about: Beethoven’s last symphony is one of the pinnacles of Western music. The first movement emerges from bare open fifths into titanic struggle. The scherzo is thunderous and driving, with famous timpani octaves, and the Adagio is a serene set of double variations of great tenderness. The finale begins with a dissonant fanfare, after which the cellos and basses reject fragments of the earlier movements in a recitative before introducing the ‘Ode to Joy’. The deliberately simple melody grows into a choral hymn to human brotherhood, passing through a Turkish march, a solemn slow section and a double fugue to a jubilant coda.
125.ctx: Beethoven had wanted to set Schiller’s ‘Ode to Joy’ since his youth in Bonn, and sketches for the symphony date back to 1817; it was eventually commissioned by the Philharmonic Society of London. By the premiere on 7 May 1824 at the Kärntnertortheater he was completely deaf. He stood beside the conductor, Michael Umlauf, and at the end the contralto Caroline Unger turned him to face the audience so that he could see its applause. The symphony was dedicated to King Frederick William III of Prussia. Its ‘Ode to Joy’ melody is now the anthem of the European Union, and the manuscript is listed in UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register.

126.about: Six bagatelles that Beethoven conceived as a cycle, with keys descending in thirds. They range from gentle, songful pieces to fierce, explosive scherzos: the second is a burst of angry energy, the fourth a rough, stamping dance, and the last opens and closes with a brief, violent flourish framing a tender Andante. Though short, they have the depth and concentration of the late sonatas.
126.ctx: Written in 1824, the year of the Ninth Symphony’s premiere, the Op. 126 bagatelles were Beethoven’s last major work for solo piano. He told his publisher they were probably the best pieces of their kind he had written, and he intended them to be played as a set. Unlike his earlier bagatelles, several of which were gathered from old sketches, these were composed together as a unified cycle. They were published in 1825 by Schott.

127.about: The first of the late quartets opens with grand, majestic chords that return twice to punctuate a lyrical, flowing Allegro. The heart of the work is the Adagio, a set of variations of great depth on a serene, song-like theme, in which the texture constantly changes. The scherzo is rhythmic and quirky, built on a playful dotted figure and interrupted by a swift, whirling trio, and the finale has a warm, folk-like character, ending with a shimmering coda in a new, faster metre.
127.ctx: After the Ninth Symphony, Beethoven devoted his final years almost entirely to the string quartet. In 1822 the Russian prince Nikolai Galitzin, an amateur cellist, commissioned three quartets at 50 ducats each, and Op. 127 was the first to be completed, in 1825. Its premiere on 6 March 1825 by the Schuppanzigh Quartet went poorly, and Beethoven had it performed again with a different leader, Joseph Böhm, with much greater success. The late quartets baffled many of Beethoven’s contemporaries but have become touchstones for later composers.

129.about: A boisterous, humorous rondo in G major, bursting with manic energy. The cheerful main theme returns again and again, each time more wildly varied, with sudden key changes, hammering accents and scurrying runs, as if someone were turning the house upside down in search of a lost coin. It is a brilliant showpiece full of jokes, and a favourite encore.
129.ctx: The piece dates from around 1795 but was not published until 1828, the year after Beethoven’s death, and carries the opus number assigned by its publisher, Diabelli. Its famous title, ‘Rage over a lost penny, vented in a caprice’, appears on the manuscript but was probably not written by Beethoven. The manuscript was left unfinished and was completed by another hand for publication. In 1835 Robert Schumann wrote a delighted review, declaring that it would be hard to find anything merrier.

130.prem: 21 March 1826, Vienna (Schuppanzigh Quartet, with the Grosse Fuge as finale)
130.about: A six-movement quartet of great variety. A first movement that alternates slow and fast music is followed by a tiny, flickering Presto, a gently humorous Andante, and a German dance in the style of a country Ländler. The fifth movement is the Cavatina, a song so moving that Beethoven said nothing he had written had ever affected him so deeply. The finale was originally the Grosse Fuge, a massive and dissonant fugue; Beethoven later replaced it with a lighter, more conventional Allegro.
130.ctx: Op. 130 was the third of the quartets commissioned by Prince Nikolai Galitzin. At its premiere on 21 March 1826 by the Schuppanzigh Quartet, the audience demanded repeats of two of the middle movements but found the Grosse Fuge baffling. The publisher Matthias Artaria persuaded Beethoven to write a new finale and to publish the fugue separately, and the replacement, composed in the autumn of 1826, was the last music Beethoven completed. The Cavatina was included on the Voyager Golden Record sent into space in 1977.

131.about: A quartet of seven movements played without a break. It opens with a slow, searching fugue that Wagner described as the most melancholy thing ever expressed in music, and moves through a wide range of emotions: a light, dancing Allegro, brief recitative-like interludes, a long central set of variations, a quicksilver Presto and a short, sorrowful Adagio, before a fierce, driving finale. Beethoven considered it his greatest quartet.
131.ctx: Composed in 1825–26 and published after Beethoven’s death, Op. 131 was not part of the Galitzin commission; Beethoven wrote it simply because he had more to say in the genre. He dedicated it to Baron Joseph von Stutterheim, the officer who had helped his nephew Karl enter the army after Karl’s attempted suicide in 1826. Later composers admired it above almost any other quartet; Schubert is said to have asked to hear it in his last days, although the story is uncertain.

132.about: A five-movement quartet whose centre is the ‘Heiliger Dankgesang’, a hymn of thanksgiving written in the old Lydian mode, its slow, chorale-like phrases alternating with livelier sections marked ‘Feeling new strength’. Around it are an intense, restless first movement, a gentle, dance-like scherzo with a rustic trio, a brief march, and a passionate finale in A minor whose surging theme, first sketched for the Ninth Symphony, finally breaks into A major.
132.ctx: Beethoven composed the quartet in 1825 as the second of the three commissioned by Prince Nikolai Galitzin, a Russian nobleman and amateur cellist, but work was interrupted when he fell seriously ill that spring. On recovering, he wrote the central movement, headed ‘Holy song of thanksgiving of a convalescent to the Deity, in the Lydian mode’. The quartet was published in 1827, after Beethoven’s death, and its hymn has become one of the most admired movements in all chamber music.

133.about: A massive, dissonant double fugue, originally the finale of the Quartet Op. 130. After a brief, fragmentary ‘Overtura’ that previews its themes, the fugue subject is hurled out in jagged, leaping rhythms and developed with violent energy and harsh harmonies, interrupted by a gentle, lyrical episode before the struggle resumes. It was so advanced that many listeners of the time found it incomprehensible; Stravinsky later called it ‘an absolutely contemporary piece of music that will be contemporary forever’.
133.ctx: Beethoven wrote the fugue in 1825 as the finale of Op. 130. After its puzzling reception at the premiere on 21 March 1826, he agreed to replace it and published the fugue separately in 1827, together with a version for piano four hands (Op. 134). It was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph. The manuscript of the four-hand version, long thought lost, was rediscovered in 2005 in a seminary library in Pennsylvania and sold at auction for over £1 million.
