135.about: Beethoven’s last complete quartet is compact and classical in proportion, almost Haydnesque in its wit. The first movement is light and conversational, and the Vivace scherzo is full of rhythmic jokes, with a trio that erupts into a wild, obsessively repeated frenzy. The Lento assai is a short, deeply felt song of great calm. The finale is headed ‘Der schwer gefasste Entschluss’ (The difficult decision): a slow, questioning motif, ‘Muss es sein?’ (Must it be?), is answered by a cheerful ‘Es muss sein!’ (It must be!).
135.ctx: The ‘Muss es sein?’ motto grew out of a joking canon Beethoven wrote about Ignaz Dembscher, an amateur who was told he must pay up before he could borrow the parts of Op. 130. Beethoven completed the quartet in October 1826 at Gneixendorf, where he was staying with his brother Johann, and it was published after his death with a dedication to his friend Johann Nepomuk Wolfmayer, a cloth merchant and patron. Milan Kundera made the motto a theme of his novel The Unbearable Lightness of Being.
parts: Der schwer gefasste Entschluss: Grave – Allegro
‘Must it be?’ answered by ‘It must be!’
facts: Milan Kundera used its motto in The Unbearable Lightness of Being.
The motto originated in a joke about a debt.
It was completed in Gneixendorf in 1826.

2/1.about: The sonata that opens Beethoven’s canon of thirty-two is compact, argumentative and in a minor key. Its first theme is a ‘Mannheim rocket’ — a rising arpeggio borrowed from the orchestral style of the day — and the whole Allegro grows from that gesture and its sighing answer, with a terseness that recalls the finale of Mozart’s G-minor Symphony. The Adagio is a gentle, ornamented aria adapted from a piano quartet Beethoven had written as a teenager in Bonn. The Menuetto keeps the minor-key shadow, with a flowing trio in F major. The Prestissimo finale is a whirl of pounding triplets, interrupted by a long, calm, song-like episode in A-flat before the storm returns.
2/1.ctx: Beethoven reached Vienna in November 1792 to study with Haydn. The three Op. 2 sonatas were composed during his first years there and published by Artaria in 1796 with a dedication to Haydn — a public courtesy that masked a cooler private relationship, as Beethoven felt he was learning little and had secretly taken extra counterpoint lessons from Johann Schenk. By presenting three large four-movement sonatas, like symphonies, rather than the shorter sonatas common at the time, he made a claim to seriousness. He had already played them in the salon of Prince Karl Lichnowsky, where Haydn is said to have heard them.
parts: Sonata form built from a rising ‘rocket’ arpeggio; terse and restless.
A gracious, ornamented song adapted from his early Piano Quartet WoO 36.
A shadowy minuet with a smoother trio in F major.
A stormy finale of pounding triplets, relieved by a calmer middle episode.
facts: The Adagio reuses material from the Piano Quartet WoO 36 No. 3, written in Bonn around 1785.
Its opening ‘rocket’ figure is often compared with the finale of Mozart’s Symphony No. 40.
This is the only Op. 2 sonata in a minor key.

2/2.about: The A-major sonata is the most playful and brilliant of Op. 2. The opening Allegro vivace tosses its first theme between registers with wide leaps and plunges into distant keys, with a stormy passage of broken octaves in the development. At its heart is the Largo appassionato in D major, a solemn, hymn-like melody sustained over a staccato bass that imitates a cellist’s pizzicato. The third movement is Beethoven’s first piano-sonata scherzo, quick and witty with a sombre A-minor trio. The finale is a graceful rondo whose theme opens with a flamboyant upward arpeggio, decorated differently at each return, with a fierce A-minor episode of driving triplets at its centre.
2/2.ctx: Written in 1794–95, this sonata reflects the young Beethoven’s success as a performer in aristocratic salons, where he was admired above all for his improvisation. Carl Czerny, his later pupil, remembered his playing as remarkable for its legato and power — qualities the wide-ranging textures of this sonata demand. The Viennese pianos of the day, by makers such as Anton Walter, had a range of barely five octaves, and Beethoven already writes at their limits. The Largo’s staccato bass shows an early interest in imitating string and orchestral effects on the keyboard.
parts: Playful sonata form full of leaps and sudden changes of direction.
A hymn-like melody over detached, staccato bass notes.
Beethoven’s first piano sonata scherzo: light and quick-witted.
An elegant rondo with a flamboyant opening flourish and a stormy A-minor episode.
facts: The Largo appassionato is Beethoven’s first slow movement to carry the marking ‘appassionato’.
It contains the first movement titled ‘Scherzo’ in his piano sonatas.
Henle lists it at ABRSM Grade 7 level.

2/3.about: The C-major sonata is the most virtuosic of Op. 2 and the one most like a concerto. Its first movement, whose main themes come from Beethoven’s unpublished Bonn Piano Quartet in C, is packed with broken octaves, trills and double thirds, and near the end it pauses for a written-out cadenza, just as a concerto would. The Adagio moves to the distant key of E major, alternating a serene, hymn-like theme with a turbulent E-minor section. The Scherzo is built on a playful figure passed between the voices, and the finale is a brilliant rondo of leaping chords and runs of sixths, with a warm, chorale-like episode and a sparkling close full of trills.
2/3.ctx: In his first Vienna years Beethoven’s reputation rested on his playing, and this sonata was plainly written to display it. Contemporary accounts describe how he overwhelmed listeners at the keyboard and, in the years that followed, competed against rival virtuosos such as Joseph Wölfl and Daniel Steibelt in improvisation contests. The careful imitative writing of the scherzo shows his counterpoint studies with Johann Georg Albrechtsberger at work. Its brilliant passagework made the sonata a staple for nineteenth-century virtuosos, and it remains a favourite in competitions.
parts: Sonata form in concerto style, with rapid double thirds and a written cadenza.
A deeply felt slow movement with a dramatic E-minor middle section.
A lively, imitative scherzo with a swirling trio.
A brilliant finale of chord leaps and running figures, with a songful middle episode.
facts: The first movement includes a written-out cadenza, a concerto feature rare in a solo sonata.
Its Adagio is in E major, a distant key relative to C major.
Like Op. 2 No. 1, it reuses material from the Bonn piano quartets WoO 36.

10/1.about: The first of the three Op. 10 sonatas is compressed and fiery, in C minor, the key Beethoven reserved for turbulent, heroic music. The opening Allegro molto e con brio slams upward in dotted chords, answered by a gentle, pleading phrase; this contrast of force and tenderness drives the whole lean movement, in which the silences between the explosive chords matter as much as the notes. The Adagio molto in A-flat major is a long, richly ornamented song in the manner of an operatic aria. The short Prestissimo finale is nervous and full of sudden pauses, briefly outlining a rhythm that anticipates the Fifth Symphony, and it fades away in C major rather than ending in triumph.
10/1.ctx: Published in 1798, the three Op. 10 sonatas were dedicated to Countess Anna Margarete von Browne, wife of Count Johann Georg von Browne, an officer in Russian service and one of Beethoven’s most generous early patrons. Ferdinand Ries recalled that the count once gave Beethoven a horse, which he promptly forgot about until a large feed bill arrived. C minor had special significance for Beethoven — the key of the ‘Pathétique’, the Third Piano Concerto, the Fifth Symphony and Op. 111 — and Mozart’s C-minor Fantasia and Sonata, K. 475/457, are often seen as models. The Leipzig Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung praised the sonatas’ ideas but complained of an overloaded, sometimes bizarre style.
parts: Fierce, rising chords answered by gentle, pleading phrases.
A short, nervous finale that fades away in the major.
facts: Its finale contains an early hint of the Fifth Symphony’s famous rhythm.
Ferdinand Ries recalled that Count Browne once gave Beethoven a horse, which he promptly forgot about.
Henle rates it level 7 (ABRSM ARSM).

10/2.about: The shortest and most humorous of the Op. 10 sonatas, full of Haydnesque wit. The first movement opens with a teasing, stop-start theme and later begins its recapitulation in the ‘wrong’ key of D major before sliding back to F — a joke that only works if the listener knows what to expect. There is no real slow movement: instead comes an Allegretto in F minor, a smooth, shadowy piece with a warm, chorale-like trio in D-flat major. The Presto finale is a brilliant, contrapuntal romp in which a chattering theme is tossed from voice to voice like a playful fugue, exposing every unevenness in the fingers.
10/2.ctx: Composed in 1796–97, this sonata shows Beethoven’s debt to Haydn’s humour, even as his relationship with his former teacher was cooling. Its jokes depend on familiarity with classical conventions — the false recapitulation is funny only if one expects the true one — and a Viennese audience steeped in Haydn’s symphonies and quartets would have caught them at once. Czerny stressed that the finale needs great lightness and precision. The sonata’s brevity and wit have made it a favourite for teaching.
parts: Witty sonata form with a mischievous false return in D major.
A dark, legato minuet-like movement with a warm D-flat trio.
A quick finale of chattering imitative entries.
facts: The first movement’s recapitulation begins in D major rather than the home key of F.
It has no true slow movement.
Henle rates it level 7.

10/3.about: The D-major sonata is the most ambitious of Op. 10 and one of the pivotal works of Beethoven’s early career. Its opening Presto is built almost entirely from a four-note descending figure, developed with relentless energy — a technique that would become central to his mature style. The Largo e mesto (‘slow and sad’) in D minor is the emotional centre and one of the most profound tragic movements he had yet written: dark chords, sighing phrases and painful dissonances build to a climax before the music sinks into a hollow, fragmented close. The Menuetto offers gentle consolation, with a rushing trio of hand-crossings, and the finale is an eccentric rondo built on a questioning three-note figure, full of pauses and surprises, that ends quietly.
10/3.ctx: Composed in 1797–98, the sonata dates from the years when Beethoven was consolidating his reputation in Vienna and first noticing the ringing in his ears that he would confide to friends in 1801. According to Anton Schindler, Beethoven said the Largo portrayed the state of mind of a melancholic, with all its nuances of light and shade; Schindler’s reports are often unreliable, but the description fits. Czerny and later writers regarded it as the most important of the early sonatas after the ‘Pathétique’, and it has been championed by pianists from Artur Schnabel, who made the first complete recording of the sonatas in the 1930s, to the present day.
parts: A driving movement built almost entirely from its opening four-note figure.
A grief-stricken lament with painful dissonances and sudden outbursts.
A gentle minuet with a rushing, hand-crossing trio.
A playful rondo that keeps asking a three-note question.
facts: Henle uses this sonata as its reference example for level 7.
The Largo e mesto is often considered Beethoven’s first great tragic slow movement.
The first movement is built almost entirely from its opening four-note motif.

14/1.about: An intimate, lyrical sonata in E major, in three movements. The first opens with a gentle rising fourth and flowing, overlapping voices, like a conversation between string players, and its development moves through several keys without ever becoming dramatic. The middle movement, an Allegretto in E minor, is wistful and restless, with a C-major trio. The finale is a flowing rondo, Allegro comodo, carried along by gentle triplet rhythms. There are no great climaxes: the sonata is a study in understatement and the interplay of voices, approachable yet so transparent that it leaves nowhere to hide.
14/1.ctx: Composed in 1798 and published in 1799, the two Op. 14 sonatas were dedicated to Baroness Josefa von Braun, wife of the director of the Vienna court theatres. In 1801–02 Beethoven arranged this sonata for string quartet, transposing it to F major. At the time he complained to his publisher about poor, unauthorised arrangements of his piano works, insisting that only the composer, or someone equally skilled, could make such transcriptions properly. His own arrangement shows how naturally the sonata’s textures translate to strings, and it is still occasionally performed.
parts: A gentle, lyrical movement with overlapping voices.
A wistful, minuet-like movement with a C-major trio.
A flowing, good-humoured rondo with running triplets.
facts: Beethoven arranged it for string quartet in F major (Hess 34).
Henle lists it at ABRSM Grade 8 level.
The Op. 14 sonatas were dedicated to Baroness Josefa von Braun.

14/2.about: A cheerful, lighthearted sonata in G major, also in three movements. The first movement plays tricks with its rhythm, its syncopated opening obscuring where the downbeat lies and keeping the listener guessing about the metre. The middle movement is a set of variations on a crisp, march-like theme in C major, each adding a new layer of rhythmic activity. The finale is a humorous rondo labelled Scherzo, full of rhythmic displacements, which ends with a quiet, deadpan cadence — a joke that works best when played with complete seriousness.
14/2.ctx: Composed and published in 1799 alongside its companion, the sonata was dedicated to Baroness Josefa von Braun. Schindler claimed that Beethoven described both Op. 14 sonatas as dialogues between two principles, a pleading voice and a resisting one; whether true or not, the idea suits the conversational character of the music. Its humour reflects the influence of Haydn, whose sonatas and trios Beethoven knew well. It was one of the first of his sonatas to enter the teaching repertoire, where its clear textures and moderate difficulty keep it a favourite.
parts: Genial sonata form with rhythmic sleight of hand.
Variations on a staccato, march-like theme.
A rondo in scherzo style that ends with a pianissimo punchline.
facts: Its finale is titled Scherzo but written in rondo form.
Schindler reported Beethoven describing the Op. 14 sonatas as dialogues between two characters.
Henle lists it at ABRSM ARSM level.

27/1.about: The first of two sonatas Beethoven titled ‘Sonata quasi una fantasia’ (sonata in the manner of a fantasy), with four movements that run together without breaks. A simple, gentle Andante frames a sudden, boisterous Allegro, creating a sense of spontaneity. The second movement is a shadowy C-minor scherzo of rolling triplets and syncopations. A short, songful Adagio con espressione in A-flat grows directly into the finale, a lively Allegro vivace that recalls the Adagio’s theme before a quick Presto coda. That cyclic return was a significant step towards Beethoven’s later unified designs.
27/1.ctx: Composed in 1800–01 and published in 1802 alongside the ‘Moonlight’, the sonata was dedicated to Princess Josephine von Liechtenstein. Beethoven’s title ‘quasi una fantasia’ suggests he wanted listeners to hear these sonatas as freer and more improvisatory than traditional ones, reflecting his reputation as a great improviser. Less famous than its companion, the sonata is a remarkable experiment, and its continuous structure anticipates later works such as the Sonata Op. 101 and the String Quartet Op. 131.
parts: A simple, gentle theme framing a sudden, lively Allegro.
A shadowy scherzo of rolling triplets.
A short, songful Adagio leading directly into the finale.
A lively finale in which the Adagio theme returns before a quick coda.
facts: The Adagio theme returns in the finale, a cyclic idea.
The movements are played without breaks.
Henle rates it level 8, higher than the Moonlight Sonata.

27/2.about: The most famous of all Beethoven’s sonatas begins with its slow movement: a hushed, rocking triplet accompaniment beneath a sparse, repeated-note melody, played with the dampers raised throughout (‘senza sordino’) to create a hazy, sustained sound. A graceful Allegretto in D-flat major follows, which Liszt called ‘a flower between two abysses’. The finale, Presto agitato, is one of Beethoven’s most intense movements, a tempestuous storm of surging arpeggios and sharp accents in full sonata form. The sonata moves from stillness to fury, reversing the usual classical order and placing its weight at the end.
27/2.ctx: Composed in 1801 and published in 1802, the sonata was dedicated to Countess Giulietta Guicciardi, a young pupil with whom Beethoven was briefly in love; she married Count Wenzel Robert von Gallenberg in 1803. The nickname ‘Moonlight’ came in 1832, five years after Beethoven’s death, when the critic Ludwig Rellstab compared the first movement to moonlight on Lake Lucerne. The sonata made Beethoven a household name among amateur pianists, and Czerny reported that he was irritated by the first movement’s popularity, remarking that he had written better things. It remains among the most recognisable pieces of classical music.
parts: Rocking triplets beneath a quiet, repeated-note melody, to be played with the dampers raised.
A delicate minuet-like interlude — ‘a flower between two abysses’, as Liszt put it.
A tempestuous sonata-form finale of surging arpeggios and sharp accents.
facts: The nickname dates from 1832, after Beethoven’s death.
Beethoven asked for the first movement to be played with the dampers raised throughout.
Henle lists it at ABRSM ARSM level.

31/1.about: The G-major sonata is Beethoven’s most openly comic piano work. In the first movement the right hand repeatedly arrives a fraction before the left, as if the pianist cannot coordinate, and the second theme appears in the ‘wrong’ key of B major — a bold harmonic stroke disguised as a joke. The Adagio grazioso is a long, deliberately over-decorated aria in 9/8, with trills, runs and cadenzas that gently parody the florid Italian operatic style, yet it is also genuinely beautiful. The finale is a relaxed, songful rondo whose coda plays games with tempo, alternating hesitant Adagio fragments with a Presto dash to the end.
31/1.ctx: According to Czerny, in 1802 Beethoven told his friend Wenzel Krumpholz that he was dissatisfied with his previous works and would take a ‘new path’. The three Op. 31 sonatas, commissioned by the Zurich publisher Hans Georg Nägeli, are often seen as the first fruits of this resolution. When this sonata appeared in 1803 it was full of errors and even contained four bars Nägeli had added to ‘correct’ Beethoven, who was furious and had Ries prepare a corrected edition with Simrock in Bonn, marked ‘Édition très correcte’. Though written in the year of the Heiligenstadt Testament, the music shows no sign of Beethoven’s despair.
parts: Deliberately ‘out of sync’ hands and abrupt key shifts.
An elaborately decorated, tongue-in-cheek operatic aria.
A good-natured rondo with a teasing, stop-start coda.
facts: The Zurich publisher Nägeli added four bars of his own, infuriating Beethoven.
A corrected edition was published by Simrock as ‘Édition très correcte’.
The second theme of the first movement is in B major, an unusual key relationship for a G-major sonata.

31/2.about: The D-minor sonata is one of Beethoven’s most dramatic and innovative. The first movement begins with a slow, questioning arpeggio, followed by an agitated Allegro; these contrasting tempos alternate throughout, blurring the line between introduction and main theme. At the start of the recapitulation the arpeggio dissolves into a haunting, pedalled recitative, like a voice speaking from far away. The Adagio in B-flat major is noble and hymn-like, with drum-like rumbles in the bass. The finale is a flowing perpetual motion in 3/8 built on a single rhythmic figure — Czerny said it was inspired by a horse galloping past Beethoven’s window — and it fades quietly into silence.
31/2.ctx: The nickname ‘Tempest’ comes from Anton Schindler, who claimed that when he asked Beethoven about the meaning of this sonata and the ‘Appassionata’, Beethoven replied, ‘Just read Shakespeare’s Tempest.’ Scholars doubt the story, but the name has stuck because it suits the music’s turbulent character. The sonata was published by Nägeli in 1803 together with Op. 31 No. 1. Its long pedal markings in the recitatives were so unusual that later editors often changed them, though on the pianos of Beethoven’s time, with less sustain, the effect would have been less blurred.
parts: Hesitant arpeggios alternate with urgent drive; recitative passages speak without words.
A serene movement with drum-like rumbles in the bass.
A continuous, whirling finale said to have been inspired by a galloping horse.
facts: The ‘Tempest’ nickname comes from a doubtful anecdote by Schindler.
Beethoven’s long pedal markings in the recitatives were often ‘corrected’ by later editors.
Henle lists it at ABRSM LRSM level.

31/3.about: The E-flat sonata is genial and humorous, with no true slow movement. The first movement begins with a questioning phrase on a dissonant chord, as if starting mid-conversation, and only gradually finds its way to the home key; its lively second theme and brilliant passagework give it a sunny character. The second movement is a scherzo in 2/4, staccato and full of dry humour, unusually cast in sonata form. The third is a gentle, songful minuet, one of the last in his sonatas. The finale, Presto con fuoco, is a galloping, tarantella-like movement that suggests a hunt, giving the sonata its nickname ‘La Chasse’.
31/3.ctx: Composed in 1802, the sonata was published by Nägeli in 1804, separately from its two companions. Together, the Op. 31 sonatas show Beethoven experimenting with structure and character on his ‘new path’, paving the way for the ‘Waldstein’ and the ‘Appassionata’, and this one reveals the humorous, energetic side of him that is often overshadowed by his more dramatic works. The minuet’s theme later caught the attention of Camille Saint-Saëns, who used it in his Variations on a Theme of Beethoven for two pianos, Op. 35 (1874).
parts: Opens mid-thought, with a question answered by warm cadences.
A staccato scherzo in 2/4 time, full of dry humour.
A gentle, songful minuet with a chordal trio.
facts: The minuet is the last Beethoven wrote in a piano sonata.
Saint-Saëns used the minuet as the theme of his Variations for two pianos, Op. 35.
It has no slow movement.

49/1.about: A short, two-movement sonata, gentle and melancholy, written for students. The first movement, an Andante in G minor, is a tender, flowing piece in sonata form, its melody moving mostly in steps over a simple accompaniment; the challenge is to shape its long phrases while keeping the left hand quiet. The second movement is a cheerful rondo in G major, with a crisp, dancing theme of repeated notes and quick turns that rewards clean finger work. Though simple, the sonata is written with care and offers young pianists a good introduction to Beethoven’s style.
49/1.ctx: Beethoven probably wrote the two Op. 49 sonatas in the late 1790s for his pupils and never intended them for publication. His brother Caspar Carl, who handled some of his business affairs, sold them to a Viennese publisher in 1805, which is why they carry an opus number much later than their composition. Although small, they are genuine Beethoven, and pianists such as Artur Schnabel and Wilhelm Kempff included them in their complete recordings of the sonatas. They remain among the most widely taught of all his works.
parts: A tender, flowing movement in sonata form.
A lively rondo with a crisp, dancing theme.
facts: Henle uses Op. 49 as its reference example for level 3.
Beethoven’s brother Caspar Carl sold them to a publisher without Beethoven’s involvement.
Composed around 1797–98, they were published in 1805.

49/2.about: A friendly two-movement sonata in G major that is a staple of piano lessons. The first movement bustles with triplets and has a cheerful, open character, demanding even fingerwork. The second is a courtly Tempo di menuetto in rondo form, with a graceful theme and contrasting episodes that teach phrasing and poise. Its minuet theme became one of Beethoven’s best-known melodies when he reused it in his popular Septet, Op. 20. Both movements are short enough to learn quickly, making the sonata a popular choice for recitals and examinations.
49/2.ctx: Composed around 1795–96, earlier than its companion, this was one of two sonatas Beethoven wrote for teaching and then put aside; his brother Caspar Carl sold both to a publisher in 1805, apparently without Beethoven’s involvement. In the meantime Beethoven had reused its minuet theme in the Septet (1799), showing that he valued the tune enough to give it a much larger stage. Today it is often a pianist’s very first Beethoven sonata.
parts: A cheerful movement driven by running triplets.
A graceful minuet-rondo, also used in the Septet.
facts: Its minuet theme also appears in the Septet, Op. 20.
Composed around 1795–96.
Henle rates it level 3.

81a.about: One of Beethoven’s few openly programmatic works. It begins with a three-note horn-call motif over which he wrote the syllables ‘Le-be-wohl’ (Farewell). The first movement moves from a tender Adagio introduction to an energetic Allegro in which the motif appears throughout; in the coda it overlaps with itself, the clashing harmonies suggesting a departing carriage fading into the distance. The slow movement, ‘Abwesenheit’ (Absence), is a restless, sighing piece of loneliness that leads straight into the finale, ‘Das Wiedersehen’ (Reunion), which bursts in with exuberant cascades of joy, pausing for a tender, slower reflection before its brisk final flourish.
81a.ctx: Archduke Rudolph, Beethoven’s pupil and patron, fled Vienna with the imperial family in May 1809 as Napoleon’s army approached, and returned in January 1810. Beethoven dated the movements to match these events, making the sonata a musical diary of friendship, and it was published in 1811 with a dedication to Rudolph. Beethoven objected when Breitkopf & Härtel used the French title ‘Les Adieux’, arguing that ‘Lebewohl’ is a heartfelt farewell to one person, while ‘adieux’ is said to a whole gathering.
parts: The ‘Lebewohl’ horn-call motif shapes a tender, then energetic movement.
A restless, sighing movement of loneliness.
Exuberant cascades of joy that lead to a quiet, glowing close.
facts: Beethoven objected to the French title ‘Les Adieux’.
The movements are dated to match Archduke Rudolph’s departure and return.
The horn-call motif is set to the syllables ‘Le-be-wohl’.

12/1.about: The first of Beethoven’s ten sonatas for piano and violin — he always named the piano first, and the keyboard part is as important as the violin’s. The D-major sonata opens with a bold unison fanfare before a flowing, lyrical theme, and the two instruments exchange material as equals rather than one merely accompanying the other. The middle movement is a set of four variations on a simple A-major theme, the third stormy and in A minor. The finale is a lively rondo in 6/8 whose syncopated accents give it a rustic flavour. Its brilliant piano writing reflects Beethoven’s own skill as a performer.
12/1.ctx: The three Op. 12 sonatas were composed in 1797–98 and published by Artaria in 1799 with a dedication to Antonio Salieri, the imperial Kapellmeister, with whom Beethoven was studying Italian vocal composition. A review in the Leipzig Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung found them ‘learned, learned and always learned’, full of strange modulations and lacking natural melody; the critic admitted the composer was a fine pianist but found the music overloaded with difficulties. Today the sonatas are admired for their freshness and wit and the way they balance the two instruments.
parts: Tema con variazioni: Andante con moto
Four variations on a simple, graceful theme.
facts: Beethoven always titled these works ‘for piano and violin’, piano first.
A 1799 review called the set ‘learned, learned and always learned’.
They were dedicated to Antonio Salieri, Beethoven’s teacher in vocal composition.

12/2.about: A playful sonata in A major with a light texture. The first movement, Allegro vivace, is a quick, humorous conversation in which a skipping theme is tossed back and forth between the instruments. The middle movement, Andante, più tosto Allegretto, is a wistful, sighing piece in A minor, its melody first given to the piano and then shared with the violin. The finale, Allegro piacevole, is a charming, relaxed rondo with a lilting theme. Its intimacy and humour make it a delight to play and to hear.
12/2.ctx: The second of Beethoven’s first set of violin sonatas, written in 1797–98 as he was establishing himself as a composer in Vienna, and dedicated with its companions to Antonio Salieri. The Op. 12 sonatas show the influence of Mozart’s violin sonatas, which Beethoven admired, and were probably aimed at skilled amateurs as well as professionals, reflecting a growing market for chamber music in Viennese homes. This is the most intimate of the three, relying on wit rather than display.
parts: A quick, humorous conversation between violin and piano.
facts: Its slow movement is in A minor, the tonic minor.
The finale is marked ‘piacevole’ (pleasant).
It is the shortest of the Op. 12 sonatas.

12/3.about: The most expansive of the Op. 12 set, in E-flat major, with a brilliant, virtuosic piano part. The first movement, Allegro con spirito, sweeps along on rapid piano figuration and scales. The Adagio con molt’espressione in C major is one of the loveliest slow movements of Beethoven’s early violin sonatas, a broad, deeply expressive song. The finale, Rondo: Allegro molto, is energetic and witty, with syncopated rhythms and dazzling passagework for both players.
12/3.ctx: Composed in 1797–98 and published in 1799 with its two companions, the sonata was dedicated to Antonio Salieri. The prominence of the piano reflects Beethoven’s own position as the pianist who performed these works, and its key of E-flat major was associated with grandeur and nobility in the classical period. Despite the critic who found them ‘learned’ to a fault, the Op. 12 sonatas were among the first of Beethoven’s chamber works to gain wide circulation.
parts: A brilliant opening with rapid piano figuration.
A deeply expressive, singing slow movement.
facts: Its slow movement is in C major, a third away from the home key.
The piano part is the most virtuosic of the Op. 12 set.
E-flat major was often associated with nobility in Beethoven’s time.

30/1.about: A gentle, lyrical sonata in A major. The first movement flows quietly, with a calm theme and delicate textures, and ends softly rather than with a flourish. The Adagio molto espressivo in D major is warm and songful, one of Beethoven’s most beautiful slow movements for violin and piano. The finale is a set of six variations on a simple, graceful theme, exploring a variety of textures and moods. Beethoven originally wrote a more brilliant finale, which he transferred to the ‘Kreutzer’ Sonata.
30/1.ctx: The three Op. 30 sonatas were composed in 1802, the year of the Heiligenstadt Testament, and published in 1803 with a dedication to Tsar Alexander I of Russia — hence their occasional nickname, the ‘Alexander’ Sonatas. Beethoven replaced this sonata’s original finale, probably because it was too brilliant for the gentle character of the rest; the discarded movement later became the finale of the ‘Kreutzer’. It is the least performed of the three, but is admired for its subtlety and understatement.
parts: Six variations on a simple theme.
facts: Its original finale became the finale of the Kreutzer Sonata.
The set was dedicated to Tsar Alexander I of Russia.
The finale is a set of six variations.

30/2.about: The most dramatic and heroic of the violin sonatas before the ‘Kreutzer’, and the only one of the Op. 30 set in four movements. The first movement, in C minor, is stormy and march-like, its tense, whispered opening erupting into violent outbursts. The Adagio cantabile in A-flat major is a broad, lyrical song, and the scherzo is humorous, with a canonic trio. The finale is fiery and restless, driven to a Presto coda. Its intensity and scale make it one of Beethoven’s most powerful chamber works.
30/2.ctx: Composed in 1802 and published in 1803 as the centrepiece of the three sonatas dedicated to Tsar Alexander I of Russia, this sonata stands alongside Beethoven’s other stormy C-minor works of the period, such as the ‘Pathétique’ Sonata and the Third Piano Concerto. It was written in the year of the Heiligenstadt Testament, and its turbulence has often been heard as a reflection of his crisis over his deafness. Many violinists regard it as the finest of the set.
parts: A songful movement with dramatic outbursts.
A playful scherzo with a canonic trio.
A fiery, energetic finale with a presto coda.
facts: It is the only one of the ten violin sonatas in C minor.
The scherzo’s trio is a canon.
It is often considered the finest of the Op. 30 set.

30/3.about: A short, cheerful sonata in G major, in three movements. The first is quick and witty, with a skittering, humorous theme and sudden accents. The middle movement, Tempo di minuetto, is a graceful, nostalgic minuet in E-flat major, tinged with melancholy. The finale is a rustic perpetual motion over drone basses, suggesting a bagpipe and a country dance, and races to a brilliant close.
30/3.ctx: The last of the three Op. 30 sonatas, composed in 1802 and dedicated to Tsar Alexander I of Russia, it shows the lighter side of Beethoven’s style in the year of the Heiligenstadt Testament. Its playful character makes a striking contrast with the drama of its C-minor companion, and its brevity and energy have made it a popular choice to end recitals.
parts: A rustic finale over drone basses.
facts: The finale imitates a bagpipe drone.
It is the shortest of the Op. 30 set.
The middle movement is a minuet rather than a slow movement.

5/1.ded: King Frederick William II of Prussia
5/1.about: One of the first sonatas to treat the cello as an equal partner to the piano rather than as a bass accompaniment. It has two movements: a spacious Adagio sostenuto introduction leading to a long and brilliant Allegro, and a lively Rondo with a playful, dancing theme. There is no separate slow movement; the introduction takes its place. The piano part is virtuosic, reflecting Beethoven’s own skill, while the cello has both lyrical and brilliant passages.
5/1.ctx: Beethoven wrote both Op. 5 sonatas during a concert tour to Berlin in 1796 for the court of King Frederick William II of Prussia, himself a keen cellist. He performed them with the court cellist, one of the Duport brothers, and the king rewarded him with a gold snuffbox filled with louis d’or. Published in 1797 by Artaria with a dedication to the king, the pair laid the foundations of the cello sonata as a genre for equal partners.
parts: A spacious introduction and an expansive, brilliant Allegro.
facts: The King of Prussia rewarded Beethoven with a gold snuffbox full of coins.
It was written for performance at the Berlin court.
It is among the first sonatas to treat cello and piano as equals.

5/2.ded: King Frederick William II of Prussia
5/2.about: A dark, dramatic sonata in G minor that opens with a long, brooding Adagio of sombre harmonies and sighing phrases. An agitated, driving Allegro follows, full of restless energy and close dialogue between the instruments. As in its companion, there is no separate slow movement. The finale is a sunny rondo in G major, full of brilliant piano writing and good humour, which turns the sonata’s darkness into light.
5/2.ctx: Written with its companion in 1796 for the Prussian court during Beethoven’s tour to Berlin, the sonata was dedicated to King Frederick William II, a keen amateur cellist. At court Beethoven also impressed listeners with his improvisations. The Op. 5 sonatas were among the earliest works of their kind in which the cello is a true partner, and they gave the cello sonata a new seriousness that Beethoven would build on in Op. 69 and Op. 102.
parts: Adagio sostenuto e espressivo – Allegro molto più tosto presto
A brooding introduction and a restless, urgent Allegro.
facts: Its slow introduction is unusually long.
The finale switches to G major.
Written in Berlin in 1796.

102/1.about: A concise, fantasia-like sonata in C major, in two parts, each beginning with a slow introduction before a vigorous Allegro. The first opens with the cello alone in a tender, improvisatory Andante before leading to a terse, energetic Allegro vivace in A minor. The second begins with a searching Adagio and a brief reminiscence of the opening, then turns to a humorous, bustling Allegro vivace in C major. Its compression and freedom point towards Beethoven’s late style.
102/1.ctx: Beethoven wrote the two Op. 102 sonatas in 1815 for the cellist Joseph Linke, who was then living in the household of Countess Marie von Erdődy, a close friend of Beethoven and a gifted pianist. The sonatas were published in 1817 with a dedication to her. On the manuscript Beethoven called this one a ‘Freie Sonate’ (free sonata), reflecting its unconventional structure. Coming after several years of low productivity, the pair mark the threshold of his late period.
parts: A gentle opening and an abrupt, energetic Allegro.
A slow introduction and a recollection of the opening before a humorous finale.
facts: Beethoven called it a ‘free sonata’.
Written for cellist Joseph Linke.
It lasts only about 15 minutes.

102/2.about: The last of Beethoven’s cello sonatas, in D major. A bold, energetic Allegro con brio opens the work with a leaping flourish. It is followed by a profound Adagio con molto sentimento d’affetto in D minor, a hymn-like lament that ranks among Beethoven’s most searching slow movements. This leads straight into the finale, a complex, angular fugue — a hallmark of his late style that puzzled early listeners.
102/2.ctx: Written in 1815, like its companion, for the cellist Joseph Linke and dedicated to Countess Marie von Erdődy, the sonata was published in 1817. It is the first of Beethoven’s late works to end with a fugue, anticipating the Hammerklavier Sonata and the late quartets. Early reviewers found it strange and difficult, and the fugue remains a challenge for performers, but it is now recognised as a pioneering work.
facts: It is the first of Beethoven’s late works to end with a fugue.
Written for cellist Joseph Linke.
Its slow movement is the only full slow movement in the five cello sonatas.

18/1.about: The first quartet in the published set is also its most ambitious. The opening Allegro con brio is built obsessively from a short, turning motif heard in unison at the start — it has been counted more than a hundred times — and shows how much drama Beethoven could squeeze from a tiny cell. The Adagio affettuoso ed appassionato in D minor is a tragic, operatic scene of great intensity, with sobbing figures and violent outbursts, ending in hushed despair. The Scherzo is quick and playful, with a wide-leaping trio, and the finale is brilliant and energetic, with running triplets and fugal passages.
18/1.ctx: The six Op. 18 quartets were commissioned by Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz, who in the same years commissioned quartets from Haydn. Although placed first in the set, this quartet was substantially revised before publication in 1801: Beethoven wrote to his friend Karl Amenda asking him not to show anyone the earlier version he had given him. Amenda recalled that when Beethoven played him the slow movement, he said it portrayed the tomb scene from Romeo and Juliet — and Beethoven’s sketches include the French words ‘il prend le tombeau’ and ‘désespoir’ (despair), confirming the Shakespearean connection.
parts: A movement saturated with its opening turn figure.
facts: Its opening motif appears over a hundred times in the first movement.
Beethoven’s sketches mention the tomb scene of Romeo and Juliet.
An earlier version sent to Karl Amenda survives.

18/2.about: An elegant, witty quartet in G major, in a courtly style. The first movement opens with graceful phrases that sound like bows and curtsies, which gave it the nickname ‘Komplimentier-Quartett’ (the ‘Compliments’ Quartet). The Adagio cantabile in C major is an ornate song that is surprisingly interrupted by a quick, dancing Allegro. The Scherzo is light and witty, and the finale, Allegro molto quasi presto, is lively and humorous, with a playful theme and sudden changes of key.
18/2.ctx: One of the six Op. 18 quartets commissioned by Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz and published in 1801. Beethoven had long avoided the string quartet, perhaps daunted by the achievements of Haydn and Mozart, and prepared carefully by studying their quartets and working at counterpoint. This quartet is often considered the most Haydnesque of the set. Its nickname, which refers to the elaborate gestures of eighteenth-century court etiquette suggested by the opening phrases, was not Beethoven’s.
parts: Graceful phrases like courtly bows and curtsies.
An ornate song with a quick, playful interruption.
facts: Its nickname refers to bows and curtsies in the opening.
The slow movement contains a fast middle section.
It is often called the most Haydnesque of the Op. 18 quartets.

18/3.about: The first of the Op. 18 quartets to be composed. It opens with a gentle rising seventh in the first violin, a surprising interval that gives the music a floating, lyrical quality, and the first movement stays warm and unassuming throughout. The Andante con moto in B-flat major is a flowing slow movement with a rich texture. The third movement is a graceful, minuet-like Allegro with a minor-key trio, and the finale is a brilliant, galloping Presto in 6/8, full of rapid passagework and surprising harmonic turns.
18/3.ctx: Written in 1798–99, this was Beethoven’s first completed string quartet, though it was placed third when the set appeared in 1801. The six Op. 18 quartets were commissioned by Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz, the music-loving aristocrat who at the same time commissioned quartets from the aging Haydn. Beethoven may have begun with this quartet because its gentle character allowed him to explore the genre without the dramatic weight of the others.
parts: A gentle, lyrical movement that opens with a rising seventh.
A graceful, minuet-like movement with a minor-key trio.
facts: It was the first of the Op. 18 quartets to be composed.
It opens with a rising seventh in the first violin.
The finale is a galloping Presto in 6/8.

18/4.about: The only minor-key quartet of Op. 18, and the most dramatic. The first movement, Allegro ma non tanto, is urgent and passionate, in Beethoven’s characteristic C-minor style. Instead of a slow movement there is a light, fugal Andante scherzoso quasi Allegretto. The third movement is a stormy, heavily accented minuet, and the finale is a spirited rondo with a gypsy-flavoured theme that ends in a headlong Prestissimo.
18/4.ctx: One of the six Op. 18 quartets commissioned by Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz and published in 1801. It is the only quartet in the set for which no sketches survive, which has led some scholars to suggest that parts of it date from earlier in Beethoven’s career. Its C-minor intensity links it with the ‘Pathétique’ Sonata and the Piano Trio Op. 1 No. 3, and it has always been one of the most popular of the set.
parts: A light, fugal movement in place of a slow movement.
facts: It is the only minor-key quartet of Op. 18.
No sketches survive for it.
It has no slow movement.

18/5.about: A graceful quartet in A major closely modelled on Mozart’s quartet in the same key, K. 464. Like its model, it places the minuet second and follows it with a set of variations. The first movement is lively and in 6/8 time. The Andante cantabile is a set of five variations on a simple theme in D major, ending with a mysterious coda. The finale is fleet and contrapuntal.
18/5.ctx: One of the six Op. 18 quartets commissioned by Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz and published in 1801. Beethoven prepared for the genre by studying the quartets of Haydn and Mozart, and he copied out parts of Mozart’s K. 464. Czerny reported that when Beethoven looked at that score he exclaimed, ‘That’s what I call a work!’ — adding that in it Mozart had shown the world what he could do.
parts: A gentle minuet placed second, as in Mozart’s model.
Five variations on a simple theme.
facts: It is modelled on Mozart’s quartet K. 464.
Beethoven copied out Mozart’s quartet by hand.
The minuet is placed second.

18/6.about: A bright quartet in B-flat major that ends with a surprising twist. After a lively first movement, an elegant Adagio and a rhythmically tricky scherzo, the finale opens with a slow introduction titled ‘La Malinconia’ (Melancholy), full of unsettling harmonies and silences. It alternates with a carefree, dance-like Allegretto, the melancholy returning briefly before the dance wins out in a quick final rush.
18/6.ctx: The last of the six Op. 18 quartets commissioned by Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz and published in 1801. Beethoven instructed that ‘La Malinconia’ be played with the greatest delicacy (‘Questo pezzo si deve trattare colla più gran delicatezza’). It is one of the earliest works in which he gives a movement a psychological title, and its exploration of melancholy anticipates the emotional range of his later quartets.
parts: La Malinconia: Adagio – Allegretto quasi Allegro
A brooding introduction alternating with a cheerful dance.
facts: The finale’s introduction is titled ‘La Malinconia’.
Beethoven asked for it to be played with the utmost delicacy.
It is the last quartet in the Op. 18 set.

59/1.about: A vast, symphonic quartet in F major, the longest Beethoven had yet written. The first movement opens with the cello singing a broad theme over a pulsing accompaniment and unfolds on a scale comparable to the Eroica. The second movement is a strange, humorous scherzo that begins with a single repeated note on the cello. The Adagio molto e mesto in F minor is deeply mournful and leads directly, through a trill and cadenza for the first violin, into the finale, which is based on a Russian folk song.
59/1.ctx: Count Andrey Razumovsky, the Russian ambassador in Vienna and a keen amateur violinist, commissioned the three Op. 59 quartets and asked Beethoven to include Russian themes. Completed in 1806 and published in 1808, they were first played by Ignaz Schuppanzigh’s quartet. They were so novel that musicians at first found them baffling; the cellist Bernhard Romberg is said to have trampled on the part of this quartet’s second movement, thinking it a joke. On a sketch for the Adagio Beethoven wrote: ‘A weeping willow or acacia tree over the grave of my brother’.
parts: A broad theme in the cello unfolds on a symphonic scale.
A quirky scherzo built from a repeated-note rhythm.
A profound, mournful slow movement that leads into the finale.
A lively finale built on a Russian folk song.
facts: A cellist reportedly trampled the part, thinking it a joke.
Its finale is based on a Russian folk song.
It was the longest quartet written up to that time.

59/2.about: An intense, dramatic quartet in E minor. The first movement is fragmented and nervous, opening with two abrupt chords followed by a silence. The Molto adagio is a sublime, hymn-like meditation, marked ‘Si tratta questo pezzo con molto di sentimento’ (to be played with much feeling). The third movement uses a Russian theme in its trio — the same tune Mussorgsky later used in the coronation scene of Boris Godunov. The finale gallops in the ‘wrong’ key of C major, settling in E minor only at the very end.
59/2.ctx: The second of the three quartets commissioned by Count Andrey Razumovsky, who asked Beethoven to include Russian themes. Composed in 1806 and published in 1808, it was first played by Ignaz Schuppanzigh’s quartet, and a contemporary review described the set as long and difficult and not comprehensible to everyone. According to Czerny, the Adagio came to Beethoven while he was contemplating the starry sky and thinking of the harmony of the spheres.
parts: Two abrupt chords and a nervous, fragmented theme.
A hymn-like meditation, ‘to be played with much feeling’.
A syncopated scherzo with a Russian theme in the trio.
A galloping finale that starts in C major.
facts: Its Russian theme also appears in Mussorgsky’s Boris Godunov.
Czerny linked the Adagio to the starry sky.
The finale begins in C major rather than E minor.

59/3.about: A brilliant quartet in C major that begins with a mysterious slow introduction of shifting, uncertain harmonies before bursting into a bright Allegro. The second movement has a haunting, plucked cello bass beneath a melancholy tune. After a graceful, old-fashioned minuet, the finale is a thrilling, fugal perpetual motion that races to the end, a showpiece for all four players.
59/3.ctx: The last of the three quartets commissioned by Count Andrey Razumovsky, composed in 1806 and published in 1808. Unlike its companions, it contains no clearly identified Russian theme, though the second movement has an exotic, folk-like flavour. Among the sketches for its finale is a private note in which Beethoven urged himself not to let his deafness remain a secret any longer, even in his art — a sign of the determination behind the movement’s headlong energy.
parts: Introduzione: Andante con moto – Allegro vivace
A mysterious introduction and a brilliant Allegro.
A haunting, melancholy movement over pizzicato cello.
A graceful, old-fashioned minuet leading into the finale.
A thrilling fugue that races to the end.
facts: It contains no clearly identified Russian theme.
The finale is a fugue.
The minuet leads directly into the finale.

1/1.about: The first of Beethoven’s official opus numbers is a genial, confident trio in E-flat major. The opening Allegro begins with a rising arpeggio — the ‘rocket’ gesture that would recur in Op. 2 No. 1 — and unfolds with wit and energy, sharing ideas between all three instruments. The Adagio cantabile in A-flat major is a warm, songful movement with long melodies over a rippling piano accompaniment. The Scherzo begins quietly in the ‘wrong’ key before finding its way home, and the Presto finale opens with a playful leap of a tenth in the piano and races to a brilliant end.
1/1.ctx: Beethoven chose three piano trios as his official Op. 1, published by Artaria in 1795 by subscription, with Prince Lichnowsky and many Viennese aristocrats among the subscribers. The trios had already been performed at Lichnowsky’s palace, reportedly in Haydn’s presence, and the subscription earned Beethoven a substantial sum, launching his career as a published composer. Four-movement trios were unusual at the time — Haydn’s and Mozart’s usually had three — and his choice signalled an ambition to treat the genre as seriously as the symphony. This trio may date back to 1793, soon after his arrival in Vienna.
parts: A playful finale with a leaping theme.
facts: It is Beethoven’s official Op. 1, published by subscription.
The trios were performed at Prince Lichnowsky’s palace before publication.
Beethoven chose four movements, unusual for trios at the time.

1/2.about: A spacious trio in G major that opens with a slow introduction leading to an energetic Allegro vivace. The highlight is the Largo con espressione in the distant key of E major, a long, expressive slow movement of great beauty. The Scherzo is quick and light, and the Presto finale is brilliant and playful, built on a humorous, repeated-note theme that bounces between the instruments.
1/2.ctx: The second of the three trios Beethoven published by subscription as his Op. 1 in 1795, after performing them at Prince Lichnowsky’s palace. It is the longest of the set, and its slow movement is often singled out as the finest. Like its companions, it adopts the four-movement plan of the symphony rather than the three movements usual in trios by Haydn and Mozart, and it gives the violin and cello more independence than was then customary.
parts: A slow introduction and an energetic Allegro.
facts: It is the longest of the Op. 1 trios.
Its slow movement is in E major.
It opens with a slow introduction.

1/3.about: The most dramatic of the Op. 1 trios, in C minor. The first movement is passionate and urgent, opening with a brooding, questioning phrase and full of sudden dynamic contrasts. A set of five variations on a simple, song-like theme in E-flat major follows, then a stormy minuet with a gentler trio. The Prestissimo finale is fiery and driving but ends quietly, fading away in C major.
1/3.ctx: The third of the trios published as Beethoven’s Op. 1 in 1795. According to Ferdinand Ries, Haydn advised Beethoven not to publish it, fearing audiences would not understand it; Beethoven suspected him of jealousy, and it became the most admired of the set. C minor was already Beethoven’s key for turbulent music, and the trio looks forward to the ‘Pathétique’ and the Fifth Symphony. Beethoven later arranged it as a string quintet, Op. 104.
parts: Five variations on a simple theme.
A fiery finale that ends quietly in C major.
facts: Haydn reportedly advised against publishing it.
Beethoven arranged it as a string quintet, Op. 104.
It became the most successful of the three.

70/1.about: A compact, dramatic trio in D major, in three movements. The first opens with a bold, rushing unison theme, immediately contrasted with a lyrical cello melody, and races on with tremendous energy. The eerie slow movement, Largo assai ed espressivo in D minor, with its shuddering tremolos, dark harmonies and mysterious atmosphere, gave the trio its nickname ‘Ghost’. The finale is bright and energetic, dispelling the shadows.
70/1.ctx: Written in 1808 while Beethoven was staying with Countess Marie von Erdődy, a close friend and gifted pianist, to whom the two Op. 70 trios were dedicated. Czerny said the Largo reminded him of the ghost in Hamlet, and sketches for it appear alongside ideas for an opera on Macbeth, which Beethoven never wrote. The trios were published in 1809 by Breitkopf & Härtel, and E.T.A. Hoffmann reviewed them enthusiastically in 1813.
facts: Its slow movement was sketched alongside ideas for a Macbeth opera.
The dedicatee, Countess Erdődy, was a gifted pianist.
The nickname ‘Ghost’ was not Beethoven’s.

70/2.about: A warm, lyrical trio in E-flat major, in four movements. It opens with a gentle slow introduction in which the instruments enter one by one in imitation. The two middle movements are an Allegretto of double variations on two contrasting themes and a graceful, minuet-like Allegretto ma non troppo with a flowing trio. The finale is genial and expansive, full of energy and generous melody.
70/2.ctx: Composed in 1808 as the companion to the ‘Ghost’ Trio and, like it, dedicated to Countess Marie von Erdődy, the trio was published in 1809. Its relaxed, lyrical character contrasts with the drama of its partner, and it has always been played less often. E.T.A. Hoffmann’s enthusiastic 1813 review of both trios in the Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung praised their Romantic spirit and helped shape the Romantic view of Beethoven.
parts: Poco sostenuto – Allegro ma non troppo
A slow introduction and a flowing Allegro.
Double variations on two contrasting themes.
facts: E.T.A. Hoffmann praised it in an 1813 review.
It is often overshadowed by the ‘Ghost’ Trio.
Its second movement is a set of double variations.

WoO59.about: One of the most famous piano pieces ever written. The gentle, rocking A-minor theme, built on a quiet oscillation between E and D-sharp, alternates with two contrasting episodes: a sunny one in F major with flowing figuration, and a stormy one over a repeated bass note. The piece is in rondo form (ABACA), and although it is often taught as an easy piece, the episodes require good technique and control.
WoO59.ctx: The piece was published in 1867, forty years after Beethoven’s death, by Ludwig Nohl, who read the manuscript’s inscription as ‘Für Elise am 27 April zur Erinnerung von L. v. Bthvn’. Many scholars believe it was intended for Therese Malfatti, a pupil to whom Beethoven proposed marriage in 1810, and that Nohl misread ‘Therese’; others have suggested the singer Elisabeth Röckel. The manuscript has since been lost. Beethoven revised the piece in 1822, possibly for a set of bagatelles.
facts: The original manuscript is lost.
The dedicatee may have been Therese Malfatti or Elisabeth Röckel.
Beethoven revised it in 1822.

WoO80.about: A compact set of 32 variations in C minor on an eight-bar theme over a descending chromatic bass, in the tradition of the Baroque chaconne. The variations follow one another without a break, exploring brilliant figuration, dramatic contrasts and a brief, lyrical turn to C major, before an extended coda brings the work to a powerful close. It is a concise showcase of Beethoven’s pianistic and dramatic imagination.
WoO80.ctx: Composed in 1806 and published in 1807, the set was never given an opus number, suggesting Beethoven did not rate it highly. According to an anecdote passed down through the Streicher family, on hearing it played years later and learning it was his own, he exclaimed, ‘Oh Beethoven, what an ass you were!’ It has nonetheless remained a popular showpiece, admired for its concentration and variety.
facts: Beethoven reportedly disowned it in later years.
It is based on a chaconne-like bass.
Henle rates it level 7 (ABRSM ARSM).

WoO57.about: A gracious, singing rondo in F major, marked Andante grazioso con moto. Its warm, flowing melody returns several times, each time more richly decorated, and is set off by contrasting episodes that wander into distant keys. Its lyricism and elegant ornamentation made it one of Beethoven’s most popular piano pieces during his lifetime.
WoO57.ctx: It was originally written in 1803–04 as the slow movement of the ‘Waldstein’ Sonata, Op. 53. When a friend told Beethoven the sonata was too long, he replaced it with a short introduction and published this movement separately in 1805; the name ‘favori’ reflects its popularity. Ferdinand Ries recalled learning it by ear after Beethoven played it to him, then playing it to Prince Lichnowsky, who in turn played it to Beethoven as his own composition. Beethoven was so annoyed that, Ries said, he never played for Ries again.
facts: It was originally the slow movement of the Waldstein Sonata.
Its name ‘favori’ reflects its popularity.
Henle rates it level 6.

WoO39.about: A short, single-movement piano trio in B-flat major, in the form of a gentle Allegretto. Its graceful, song-like theme is shared between piano, violin and cello in easy, conversational exchanges, and the whole piece unfolds as a compact, tuneful movement. It is simple enough for a young player, but written with the warmth and polish of Beethoven’s maturity.
WoO39.ctx: Beethoven wrote the trio in June 1812 for Maximiliane Brentano, then ten years old, inscribing it to his ‘little friend M. B.’ to encourage her piano playing. She was the daughter of Antonie and Franz Brentano, close friends of Beethoven, and later received the dedication of the Piano Sonata Op. 109. The trio was published in 1830, after Beethoven’s death.
facts: Written for 10-year-old Maximiliane Brentano.
She later received the dedication of Op. 109.
It was published in 1830.

WoO81.about: A brief, lively Allemande in A major. In Beethoven’s time the name usually meant a quick German dance of the kind that filled Viennese ballrooms in the 1790s, rather than the stately Baroque allemande. It is a charming miniature with a bright, rhythmic theme.
WoO81.ctx: Beethoven sketched the Allemande in 1793, early in his Vienna years, and returned to it in 1822, when he was gathering short pieces for his late sets of bagatelles. It was not published until long after his death and remains a rarely heard curiosity among his piano works.
facts: It is one of Beethoven’s shortest piano pieces.
It was revised in 1822.
It was published posthumously.

WoO134.about: Four different settings of Goethe’s poem ‘Nur wer die Sehnsucht kennt’ (Only one who knows longing), Mignon’s song from the novel Wilhelm Meister’s Apprenticeship. Each is short, but each finds a different response to the same words, ranging from plaintive and hymn-like to more restless and flowing, so that together they read like a series of sketches exploring one emotion.
WoO134.ctx: Beethoven composed the settings in 1807–08 and published all four together in 1810, a rare chance to hear him trying out different solutions for the same text. The poem was a favourite of composers: Schubert set it six times, and Tchaikovsky’s version became one of his most famous songs.
facts: The poem comes from Goethe’s novel Wilhelm Meister.
Schubert and Tchaikovsky also set this poem.
Beethoven published all four settings together.

WoO60.about: A short, cheerful bagatelle in B-flat major, marked ‘Ziemlich lebhaft’ (fairly lively). In a single compact span it combines a bright, bustling theme with the quirky accents and abrupt turns found in Beethoven’s late piano miniatures. It makes an attractive encore or teaching piece.
WoO60.ctx: Beethoven wrote the piece in 1818, while he was working on the Hammerklavier Sonata. It was first published in 1824 in a supplement to the Berliner allgemeine musikalische Zeitung, one of the few of his short pieces to appear in a music journal, and it stands alongside the late bagatelles as a glimpse of his late style in miniature.
